title: March 4, 2026 – Customer Spotlight: Midland Fire Department Enhances Radiation Detection with SAM 950
body:
The Midland Fire Department has strengthened its emergency response capabilities by upgrading its radiation detection technology, giving firefighters faster, more accurate insight during hazardous-material incidents and other emergencies.

With the support of grant funding, the department added the Berkeley Nucleonics SAM 950 handheld radiation detection system. This SAM 950 is designed specifically for first responders, nuclear field analysts, and specialized military and security teams.

According to Lt. Tyler Alden, the new system has become a valuable operational asset.

“It is an asset. It makes our department quicker,” Alden said. “It makes our response to radiation faster.”

Bringing Radiation Detection into the Modern Era

The department received the SAM 950 in January and now shares it across stations among trained personnel. While radiation monitoring has long been part of Midland Fire’s mission, the new technology represents a major step forward.

“This equipment brings our radiation detection from the 1960s into modern day,” Alden noted.

With real-time analysis and advanced identification capabilities, responders can quickly determine what type of radiation is present and how to proceed safely.

“It tells us what kind of radiation it is,” Alden explained. “It tells us if it was medical radiation or ill intent.”

Advanced Capabilities in a Handheld Platform

The SAM 950 combines multiple critical tools into one portable system, including:

  • Radiation survey meter
  • Spectral analysis
  • Secondary screening
  • Isotope identification and confirmation
  • Source location features

These capabilities support hazmat response, medical and industrial monitoring, event security, and port and border enforcement.

By consolidating these functions into a single device, Midland firefighters can respond more efficiently and with greater situational awareness.

Rapid Training and Deployment

Firefighters trained on the SAM 950 were able to learn the system in just one day, allowing the department to deploy it quickly across multiple stations.

This rapid adoption ensures more personnel are prepared to operate the equipment when needed—improving readiness and response times.

Commitment to Safety and Innovation

By investing in modern radiation detection technology, the Midland Fire Department continues to demonstrate its commitment to public safety and operational excellence. The SAM 950 enhances the department’s ability to protect first responders and the community while staying ahead of evolving threats.

Adapted from: “Midland Fire enhances radiation detection” by Tereasa Nims, Midland Daily News, May 13, 2022.

title: November 18, 2025 – Skip the Chamber: How the SPECTRAN V6 Enables Real-Time EMI Testing Anywhere
body:
The SPECTRAN V6 Real-Time Spectrum Analyzer is transforming how engineering teams approach EMI pre-compliance testing. Conventional methodologies typically depend on slow swept analyzers and access to a shielded chamber, which can create project delays and make it difficult to identify transient issues. The V6 architecture introduces ultra-fast scanning, real-time visibility, and intelligent noise-removal tools that help engineers find problems much earlier in the design cycle.

With sweep rates up to 3 THz/s, the system can scan very wide frequency ranges in only milliseconds. Sweeping a 1 GHz band with a 120 kHz RBW achieves roughly a 1.7 ms probability of intercept, allowing emissions and short bursts to surface immediately instead of being missed between sweeps. This delivers a much clearer picture of switching noise, digital interference, and other intermittent effects.

A major advantage is the ability to run meaningful EMI pre-compliance without a shielded room. Using the Spectral Background Mask block, the analyzer records all ambient RF activity and builds a mask to remove environmental noise. This often drops the ambient spectrum by nearly 20 dB and produces a clean spectrum for DUT measurements, even in noisy environments. Tests can be done at the bench, in a lab, or even in a simple tent setup, which offers far more flexibility than the traditional chamber-only approach.

The V6 also provides a 30 ns probability of intercept in real-time mode, making it possible to capture very short events. Transients from power supplies, processors, and mixed-signal systems appear instantly. With a frequency range from 9 kHz to 140 GHz, the platform supports nearly every modern EMI and wireless application.

The software includes standard EN, CISPR, and FCC limit lines, and additional limits—such as FMC or custom profiles—can be added quickly using the built-in power limit editor. Users can also record and save spectra for documentation, before/after comparisons, reference measurements, or long-term troubleshooting.

A typical EMI setup includes the V6 analyzer, HyperLOG and BicoLOG antennas, a pre-amplifier, an OCXO timebase, and the Spectral Background Mask option, along with a high-performance PC using USB 3.2 and a Ryzen 8-core processor with 64 GB RAM. Optional shielding cubes, tripods, and compass modules help build a more complete workflow. The SPECTRAN V6 provides a much faster and more flexible method for EMI pre-compliance, allowing engineers to troubleshoot quickly, shorten redesign cycles, and work without the limitations of a dedicated chamber.

title: May 21, 2025 – Model 686 Application Note: AWGs for QKD & Quantum Sensors
body:
Introduction

In our digital age, sensitive information from financial transactions to classified government data flows through networks at an unprecedented rate. However, conventional encryption methods that rely on mathematical algorithms face an existential threat from quantum computers.

Quantum computers could easily crack these encryption codes when they become powerful enough. This encapsulates the urgency to develop quantum-resistant encryption methods. QKD stands at the forefront of this endeavor.

The laws of quantum mechanics are used not only to protect our communications and data, but also to understand the world around us at an unprecedented level of detail. Light, temperature, pressure, heat, and other things imperceptible to more traditional sensors can be measured by quantum sensors. Quantum sensors depend on the constants of nature, so their reliability never degrades; they are self-calibrating and their measurements don’t drift over time like traditional sensors do.

High performance AWGs like the Model 686 are becoming extremely popular in designing and developing these emerging breakthrough technologies.

QKD: Quantum Key Distribution

Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is a secure communication method for exchanging encryption keys known only between shared parties. It uses properties found in quantum physics to exchange cryptographic keys in a way that is provable and guarantees security. QKD enables two parties to produce and share a key used to encrypt and decrypt messages.

Key distribution on a conventional scale relies on public key ciphers that use complicated mathematical calculations requiring a prohibitive amount of processing power to break. The viability of public key ciphers, however, faces several issues, and quantum computing will render most of today’s public key encryption strategies unsafe.

QKD is different from conventional key distribution because it uses a quantum system that relies on basic and fundamental laws of nature to protect the data, rather than relying on mathematics.

QKD works by transmitting many light particles, or photons, over fiber optic cables between parties. Each photon has a random quantum state, and collectively the photons sent make up a stream of ones and zeros—qubits, the equivalent of bits in a binary system. When a photon reaches its receiving end it travels through a beam splitter, which forces the photon to randomly take one path or another into a photon collector.

The receiver responds to the original sender with data regarding the sequence of the photons sent, which the sender then compares with what was originally transmitted. Photons in the wrong beam collector are discarded; what’s left is a specific sequence of bits that can be used as a key to encrypt data. Any errors and data leakage are removed during a phase of error correction and other post-processing steps.

Photons are polarized when they oscillate in only one direction, and polarizing filters let us filter for that. Quantum mechanics has made it possible to send single photons; if the receiver holds a filter the same way as the sender’s polarization, the light passes through, and if crosswise, no photon passes—meaning each photon can be measured only once.

Quantum Key Exchange

The two parties compare notes publicly on how photons were polarized and how filters were held, discarding the cases where one used a diagonal filter and the other vertical or transverse, and building their key from what remains.

If an eavesdropper tries to read along a photon with a polarization filter, they must send a new photon onward afterward, without knowing whether they held their filter correctly. Because photons cannot be copied and can only be measured once, an eavesdropper must guess often, introducing detectable errors. Comparing individual digits of the key before use reveals whether anyone has been listening, which is what makes the quantum encryption approach effectively unbreakable.

Types of QKD

There are many types of QKD, but two main categories are prepare-and-measure protocols and entanglement-based protocols.

Prepare-and-measure protocols focus on measuring unknown quantum states and can detect eavesdropping and estimate how much data may have been intercepted.

Entanglement-based protocols rely on quantum states in which two objects are linked, so that measuring one affects the other; if an eavesdropper accesses a previously trusted node and changes something, the other parties will know.

It is difficult to implement an ideal infrastructure for QKD. It is perfectly secure in theory, but in practice, imperfections in tools such as single photon detectors create security vulnerabilities, so security analysis remains important.

Modern fiber optic cables are typically limited in how far they can carry a photon, often to around 100 km, though some groups have extended this considerably—for example, the University of Geneva and Corning Inc. constructed a system capable of carrying a photon 307 km under ideal conditions.

Another challenge of QKD is that it relies on having a classically authenticated channel of communication already established. As quantum computers become more common, however, the risk that an attacker could crack current encryption methods rises, making QKD more relevant.

QKD Attack Methods

Even though QKD is secure in theory, imperfect implementations have the potential to compromise security. For example, the phase remapping attack takes advantage of the fact that a device must allow signals to enter and exit, creating a backdoor used against methods common in many commercial QKD systems.

Another attack method is the photon number splitting attack: in practice more than one photon is often sent at a time, and extra photons could be intercepted without either party knowing. Decoy state QKD, an improvement to the BB84 protocol, mixes decoy signals in with the intended signal so both parties can detect an eavesdropper.

QKD Implementation Methods

There are two approaches to implementing QKD: discrete variable QKD (DV-QKD), which relies on single photons with encoded random data, and continuous variable QKD (CV-QKD), which plays on the wave nature of light with information encoded in the quadrature of its electromagnetic fields, read out with coherent homodyne or heterodyne detection.

Different modulation solutions exist for the transmitter side (Alice) and optical hybrid demodulators for the receiver side (Bob). One of the most technologically advanced intensity modulators is the Exail NIR-MX800, whose LiNbO3 modulation offers high bandwidth, high contrast, and ease of use.

The Model 686 and Model 685 series can drive these Electro-Optic Modulators directly to generate very short optical pulses. Their ability to generate pulses with 50 ps rise/fall time, 100 ps pulse width, and 5 Vpp amplitude allows driving the EOM without an external amplifier. Using, for example, Exail’s NIR-MX800 with the BNC Model 686, very short optical pulse widths from 100 ps can be achieved at 850 nm, 1310 nm, and 1550 nm—without an external amplifier between the AWG and the modulator.

Quantum Sensors

Quantum sensors allow us to understand the world around us at an unprecedented level of detail, improving the accuracy of how we measure, navigate, study, explore, see, and interact with the world by sensing changes in motion and electric and magnetic fields, with data collected at the atomic level.

This allows quantum sensors to make technological devices exponentially more accurate, thorough, efficient, and productive, and to be less vulnerable to signal jamming and other electromagnetic interference than conventional light- and sound-based sensors. Applications include more accurate geolocation than GPS allows, more detailed medical diagnostic imaging, safer autonomous navigation, more accurate guidance systems, mapping of underground environments, and more sensitive detection of gravitational and tectonic changes.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging

MRI quantum sensors have been around for decades: MRI machines use quantum sensors and manipulate a quantum property called spin within the body’s atoms, measuring the response of those spins to a magnetic field and transforming it into an image.

Atomic clocks are another kind of quantum sensor, in use since the 1950s to keep time in GPS satellites and define the SI unit of a second. Newer technologies make additional quantum sensors and applications possible, including nitrogen vacancy (NV) centers fabricated within diamonds.

An NV center forms when a carbon atom in a diamond’s crystal lattice is replaced by a nitrogen atom next to a vacant lattice site. The resulting defect has its own quantum spin, effectively a tiny magnet, that is sensitive enough to detect magnetic field changes tens of millions of times smaller than the strength of Earth’s magnetic field—even in the presence of that background field.

The spin can be altered by electromagnetic radiation or a magnetic field, and the NV center is also photoluminescent: lit with green light, it emits a red glow whose brightness depends on the spin state. By monitoring changes in that brightness under microwave or magnetic field excitation, researchers can measure the strength of a magnetic field—a technique called optically detected magnetic resonance.

The BNC Model 686 has been used to control the experimental pulse sequences used to manipulate single tin vacancy centers in diamond, generating narrow electrical square pulses with amplitude up to 5 Vpp to drive an electro-optical amplitude modulator and produce short laser pulses with a close to Gaussian shape and a full-width-half-maximum as narrow as 130 ps.

The Model 686 can also drive an electro-optical phase modulator to generate frequency sidebands up to about 7 GHz, enabling two optical transitions to be driven with phase-stable laser fields, while its digital output channels control acousto-optical amplitude modulators or generate trigger pulses for timing experimental sequences.

title: April 25, 2025 – The PVX-2506: It’s a Voltage Source, It’s a Current Source, It’s Everything!
body:
Hi there, my name is Cameron Simmons and I am an applications engineer here at Berkeley Nucleonics. Today I am going to do a video about one of our lesser known products—the PVX-2506. It is a hybrid voltage current pulser. We refer to it as a precision voltage pulser, and it’s got a lot of cool features that may help your application.

The PVX-2506 is what we refer to as a precision pulse generator, because we tune the overshoot and undershoot so that it never exceeds the pulse top and bottom voltage. This can be really good for semiconductor material testing because you know your material is never exposed to a voltage higher than required for your testing, and you can get great data on it. The unit can do 50 volts at 10 amps, which is extremely high for a voltage pulser of this type, so the PVX-2506 can be used to test a lot of high voltage and high current semiconductor materials.

Another great feature is that the 2506 accepts a high voltage power supply and a lower voltage power supply, so you can actually float it up to ten volts. This can be really good if that’s the voltage you want tested at, or if you just want a less noisy signal moving above ground—that will take out some of the noise and help you get cleaner data.

The cable included with the 2506 is heavy duty, with gold pads and very low inductance. It can take a lot of voltage while remaining very low inductance, so you’re not going to get any added overshoot and zero ringing, which makes this overall a very good cable for this application.

An interesting feature of the PVX-2506 is a utility section that will help you invert and copy your trigger signal, so you can take one trigger in from your source and put it into the RF logic input. You’ll get a TTL copy of that signal and an inverted TTL version of it, and either can trigger RF as well—so you can put a sinusoidal waveform in and it will create a square trigger signal. This makes testing and collecting data easier without having to have an external box that does this.

On the oscilloscope, the output of the voltage pulser is a nice clean 30 volt pulse into a 5 ohm load—no aberrations, no overshoots, very square, low noise. Zooming in on the rising edge shows the overshoot tuning at work: the top never exceeds the actual pulse top, meaning the rising and falling edges are finely tuned. The falling edge is the same—it never exceeds ground, and you can get some very clean data with this.

The output of the PVX-2506 is floating and has two voltage inputs, so you can bias it up just to reject noise if that’s what your experiment calls for—for example, running at about 30 volts to ground and then engaging the second power supply to bias it up about 10 volts further. That’s the PVX-2506.

title: April 4, 2025 – The PVX-4141 at the Facility for Rare Isotope Beams
body:
Introduction

It is a great treat to learn about the ways in which our equipment from Berkeley Nucleonics has improved applications, driven solutions, and provided answers for research teams at some of the most decorated institutions across the world. Most recently, we’ve touched base with a researcher at the Facility for Rare Isotope Beams (FRIB) following their purchase and use of the PVX-4141 bipolar pulse generator, involved in the design and testing of a fast machine protection system and chopper monitor system.

In this operation, the PVX-4141 is tested for use in a linear accelerator to verify that the bipolar pulse generator works fast enough for the intensive operations at FRIB—and it does. Here is a quick synopsis of what this type of rigorous unit testing entails, from its beginning concepts to its conclusion.

Design

The design of the system is relatively common. The IOC/OPI is the user interface: the user can set threshold values, different beam modes, and verify that each element of the system is working as intended.

The chopper monitor system takes analog information from the PVX-4141 and other parts of the accelerator systems, digitizes it, and uses an FPGA to compensate for small changes in the beam in real time. This is done by modulating the frequency and width of the gate signal controlling the PVX-4141’s pulse width and repetition rate—in other words, the PVX voltage monitor and current monitor provide the data used to maintain stable operation.

Pulse Checker

The signal from the PVX-4141 is not static: the width and frequency are “ramped,” or slowly increased in a linear fashion, in different phases. The pulse checker monitors the ramp rate and ensures it is behaving correctly.

Voltage and Current Monitor

The voltage monitor (VMON) and current monitor (IMON) feed into the ADC and are processed by the FPGA, which performs the math on the received digital data. To read the very fast current pulses, the IMON signal is integrated with a capacitor during the rising edge, reset before the falling edge, then reset again afterward before the next pulse—creating a clear, readable signal for the FPGA to measure the current flowing in and out of the plates that accelerate the particle beam.

Test in Beam Line

In the validation results, a green status line moves from “beam started” to “beam on.” A red fault line rising from zero causes the green line to indicate the beam stopping, then off. This test verified that the beam auto-shutdown works, and that the time it takes the PVX-4141 to react to the error is short enough to stop any damage from taking place.

Conclusion

This exercise highlights the PVX-4141’s aptitude for integration in scientific testing and research. This model, as well as the entire PVX line, is already set up so that useful information for automation and real-time feedback is available—making it an ideal candidate for use in large, complex systems where every aspect must be measured and monitored.

title: March 18, 2025 – Multi- and Single- Channel Analyzer Options
body:
What is a Multichannel Analyzer?

Multichannel Analyzers (MCAs) constitute essential components in spectroscopy systems. An MCA comprises two primary elements: the analog-to-digital converter (ADC) and computer-addressable memory. Berkeley Nucleonics provides multiple MCA options, enabling users to configure systems aligned with their specific application requirements.

The Model 970: Portable Multichannel Analyzer

This MCA distinguishes itself through flexible architecture accommodating diverse applications—functioning as a process monitor, standalone laboratory instrument, or integrated system component for analysis. The unit offers modular assembly, compact packaging, and intuitive software, supporting applications across both spectroscopy and spectrometry domains.

TOPAZ-Pico

Advanced digital electronics underpin the TOPAZ-pico design, establishing it as a fully digital, compact, standalone advanced MCA. The unit incorporates a miniaturized high-voltage power supply optimized for low consumption, delivering 0 to 1,500 volts in 4096 steps to power PMT tubes, with two data acquisition modes supporting operational flexibility.

PHA acquisition mode offers spectral memory size options of 256, 512, 1024, 2048, and 4096 channels; coarse gain with amplification factors of 1, 2, 4, and 8; fine gain adjustment from 1 to 2 in 1/4096 increments; and upper and lower level discriminator settings configured in channels.

MCS acquisition mode offers the same spectral memory size options, dwell time adjustment from 0.1 seconds to count-forever, and simplified setup via regions of interest or nuclide information.

bPAD Compact Single Channel Analyzer

Particularly suited for count rate monitoring within specific energy regions of interest, this unit incorporates a programmable high-voltage power supply with output voltage settable from 0 to 1500 volts. title: March 7, 2025 – Big Physics: Model 765 Pulse Generator Application Note
body:
Photomultiplier Characterization and Calibration

In big physics experiments, the use of photomultipliers is fundamental and common. The photomultiplier converts an electrical charge for an acquisition system, allowing photons to be detected. The emission of photons can be correlated to a specific phenomenon studied by physicists, such as the Cherenkov effect.

During the design and production of a photomultiplier, it is necessary to characterize and calibrate it using a laser or an LED diode. The light source must be driven by a preassigned signal with a fixed width and sequence. Using the Model 765 pulse generator from Berkeley Nucleonics, it is now easier than ever to generate a pulse with various widths, periods, and amplitudes. Setup is intuitive and easy: setting a single pulse puts the instrument waiting for an external trigger-in, or it can generate pulses continuously.

Klystron Control and Synchronization

A klystron is a specialized linear-beam vacuum tube used in multiple applications—for example, in the colliders used for big physics experiments, where it generates the particles that will collide. Much like driving a light source to characterize a photomultiplier, it is necessary to generate a signal to drive the klystron.

That signal can be generated by a complex system based on a logic port or an FPGA, but the design and development of such systems is lengthy and restrictive; any sudden need to change the timing means changing the schematic or the FPGA code. The Model 765 offers an off-the-shelf solution to control and modify klystrons, with a touchscreen display that lets users simply enable signal parameters.

When driving a klystron, the user can also synchronize multiple units to the Model 765. With up to 4 independent channels, the user can set independent synchronization signals with specific delays from the trigger signal—allowing multiple klystrons to be synchronized while accounting for and compensating the delay between the different driving chains.

Data Acquisition and FPGA Testing

In big physics experiments, detectors observe different physical phenomena, but the acquisition chain that collects and stores real-time data is equally important. The read-out chain is based on a hierarchic tree structure where the lowest level, near the detectors, converts digital pulses using a communication protocol to deliver information to the next level.

Usually the lowest level is composed of an FPGA system that collects the digital pulses of multiple detectors, creating a data packet to deliver to the next level via an optical link. During development of such a system, engineers usually do not have access to detectors or the entire collider, making it necessary to find easier ways to simulate the pulses detectors would generate.

Using the BNC Model 765 pulse generator, it is possible to test the response of an FPGA system and ensure its timing and synchronization settings hold—for example, inspecting what happens if channels have skew, or testing the receipt of multiple pulses for glitches. The Model 765 offers up to 4 channels, each able to deliver single, double, triple, or quadruple pulses, with each pulse independently set for period, width, and delay relative to the trigger-in signal.

title: February 25, 2025 – Lessons from the Lab: PVX Bias
body:
This technical piece, authored by BNC electrical engineer Cameron Simmons, is excerpted from a video demonstration and addresses modifying a PVX-4151 high voltage pulse generator to enable 1,000-volt output biasing.

Device Overview

The PVX-4151 functions as a bipolar pulse generator with dual high voltage inputs for positive and negative polarity. The power supply voltages must remain within a 1,500-volt differential, though they can be asymmetrically distributed around zero—such as -500V to 1000V, -750V to 750V, or 0V to 1,500V configurations.

Design Challenge

The modification allows the device to pulse between 1,000 and 2,500 volts while respecting the differential limit. This capability serves applications like parallel-plate time-of-flight mass spectrometers, where both plates must operate at elevated voltages, with one plate pulsing slightly higher to achieve a specific particle velocity.

Technical Solution

The approach requires two positive polarity high voltage power supplies, with the lower 5 kV unit acting as bias voltage. The main complication is that most high voltage power supplies cannot independently regulate same-polarity outputs from separate sources—the higher voltage supply typically pulls the lower voltage toward its potential. A shunt resistor from the bias supply to ground maintains independent voltage regulation.

The shunt resistance follows R = Vbias / Ips, and power dissipation in capacitive loads follows P = C×V²×F. For the specific implementation, with a 50 pF capacitor connected via 2 feet of RG58 cable plus the PVX-4151’s internal 200 pF capacitance, the engineer selected a 62 megohm resistor built from soldered 10 megohm, 1-watt resistors with spade connectors and kapton tape insulation for arc prevention.

Final Outcome

The modification delivers a 1,500-volt pulse spanning from 1,000 to 2,500 volts output. Customers interested in the technique can contact Berkeley Nucleonics or visit the PVX-4151 product page for implementation assistance.

title: February 13, 2025 – Creating Tail Pulses Using the Sequencer on an Arbitrary Waveform Generator
body:
I’m Edgar, one of the engineers here at Berkeley Nucleonics, and I’m going to go over how to use our Model 670C—or any of our arbitrary waveform generators—to generate a sequence of pulses. In this case, I’m going to mimic the pulse that would come out of our BH-1, since that unit is no longer manufactured, by duplicating that signal using an arbitrary waveform generator.

Starting from the 670C’s default settings outputting a standard sine wave, I add a second entry to the sequencer—the sequencer can hold up to several thousand waveforms, depending on the application—and build a tail pulse using the exponential rise and exponential decay waveforms built into the 670C and the other Model 600 series ARBs, like the 675 and 685.

To get the required timing, I go into advanced settings and the trigger menu to set the period of the interval—in this case one millisecond, roughly one kilohertz. In Edit Entry, I set the jump sequence: sequence one to sequence two and back, set to timer, so it waits one millisecond before resetting to output the next waveform. With that in place, the unit outputs the exponential rise and exponential decay at roughly one kilohertz.

From there I set the lengths and durations of the exponential rise and exponential decay depending on the rise time and fall time I want—it’s not exact, but for example a 450 nanosecond duration and interpolation/decimation setting gets roughly a 50 nanosecond rise time, and a similar approach on the decay side—say 500 microseconds to get roughly a 100 microsecond fall time. Because this is an arbitrary waveform generator, I’m working more in terms of how many points and how long a waveform runs, rather than frequency directly, as I would with a dedicated pulse or delay generator.

That wraps up one of many ways an AWG can generate a tail pulse—the right approach generally depends on the goal and application. If you have any type of waveform you need to see, need to mimic outdated BNC equipment, or need the function of equipment no longer in production, reach out by phone or email; we can help determine whether your desired application is feasible on our arbitrary waveform generators or other products we make. Arbitrary Waveform Generators are extremely versatile, and we’re excited to push the boundaries of our units alongside your work.

title: February 7, 2025 – Non-Volatile Memory Cells Characterization
body:
The trend of memory research is to develop a new memory, Non-Volatile RAM, that joins the speed of RAM with the data retention of mass memory. There are many proposals for new cell types—FeRAM, ReRAM, MRAM, STT-MRAM, and PCM among them—each based on changing the conductivity of a material using a different physical principle. This application note describes how to test an STT-MRAM cell using a pulse generator.

MRAM Technology

MRAM memory cells use Magnetic Tunnel Junctions (MTJ) consisting of two ferromagnets separated by a thin insulator. If the magnetic fields of the two ferromagnets are oriented in the same direction, electrons can tunnel from one ferromagnet to the other through the insulator layer. The first ferromagnet has a fixed magnetic field, while the field of the second can be changed by applying a current pulse to invert its orientation, changing the conductivity of the stack.

To program or erase a bit, a current pulse is applied through the stack, and the resulting magnetic field orientation depends on the current pulse direction. The efficiency of the program-and-erase process depends on the duration and amplitude of the pulse, so it can be useful during research and development to test different combinations of pulse width and amplitude using a pulse generator that lets the user change width, amplitude, and repetition rate.

Phase Change Memory (PCM)

A PCM memory cell is based on the amorphous-to-crystalline phase change of a chalcogenide material. In the amorphous phase resistance is high, and in the crystalline phase resistance is lower. To program or erase a bit, the material’s phase must be changed: a large but low voltage pulse changes the phase from amorphous to crystalline, while a short but higher voltage pulse changes it from crystalline to amorphous—so control of pulse amplitude and width is fundamental.

The Model 765 pulse generator offers a time resolution of 10 ps and a vertical resolution of 10 mV. Newer non-volatile RAM technologies require faster pulses every year, and the Model 765—with transition times under 70 ps and amplitude up to 5 Vpp—is well suited to such requirements.

MOSFET Test

In developing modern MOSFET transistors, using high-k material for the dielectric in the MOS capacitor reduces leakage current through the isolator, but causes problems from charge trapping—voltage threshold instability, carrier channel mobility degradation, and reduced reliability. Charge trapping occurs when the transistor is in the “on” state and channel charge accumulates in an isolation layer, creating a built-in potential that changes the threshold. The degree of this effect depends on the gate stack’s thickness, dielectric type, and process technology, as well as gate voltage and pulse duty cycle, so understanding the charge trapping mechanism is important to improving the technology.

Because the timescale of this effect ranges from under 1 µs to dozens of milliseconds, DC measurements are unreliable, and different types of pulsed I-V measurements are used instead, generally falling into three categories: DC Id-Vg curves (unreliable for fast-switching devices, since results depend on charge trapping from the DC bias itself), short pulse Id-Vg curves (fast-edged, nanosecond-scale pulses that reveal an intrinsic device response before charge has time to accumulate, but give no information about the trapping phenomenon itself), and slow pulse Id-Vg curves (longer, ramped-edge pulses representative of the true Id-Vg curve, since the charge doesn’t have time to accumulate if the ramp is fast enough).

The slow pulse technique can measure drain current degradation over time to observe the trapping charge effect directly, and can also be used to predict the lifetime of switching devices by studying how charge trapping effects increase before and after switching stress. The Model 765’s fast edges, wide amplitude range, adjustable baseline offset, and pulse widths from 300 ps to 1 s make it well suited to generating the pulses needed for both short and slow pulse MOSFET characterization.

title: January 27, 2025 – Laser Driver Wire Inductance
body:
This script is authored by BNC electrical engineer Cameron Simmons, excerpted from a video demonstration.

We recently began testing transistors for a new laser driver board. During the prototyping stage something came up that seemed worth sharing.

We were testing a new MOSFET on an existing driver board, and the footprint did not line up with the chip’s pins, so we needed some kind of conductive material to connect the pins to the footprint. The obvious choice was wires similar in size to the pins.

We were getting extremely low rise times with lots of ringing and distortion, despite the MOSFET being faster than the original—clearly not going to meet the specs we needed. Something in the setup was slowing the signal down. Swapping the wires for copper tape completely fixed the problem.

The issue was the self-inductance of the wires. Comparing the self-inductance of the two methods with online calculators produced a surprising result: to match the copper tape with stranded wire, we would have needed 4 AWG cable—not remotely practical. This is a good illustration of why standard wire is a poor choice for attaching a laser diode to a driver, and why we recommend our stripline cables and output PCBs instead. A wide, flat cable facilitates a clean, fast pulse even at longer distances.

title: January 10, 2025 – Using the EVO to Prevent Damage on High Voltage Products
body:
Since acquiring Directed Energy, Berkeley Nucleonics has performed repairs on a wide range of current and former products. Because of the widespread use of DEI's high voltage pulse generators in universities and national labs, many of these repairs have involved PVX line units. When properly maintained, these units show remarkable longevity: some from the early 1990s are still functioning after minor service and recalibration, with the potential for decades more of operation.

The leading cause of PVX failures comes down to one common practice: applying the external DC high voltage too quickly.

The PVX-4110 is a good example. The unit outputs 10,000 volts with a maximum power dissipation of 100 watts. The correct procedure is to enable the unit and timing generator, then turn on the DC supply at 0V and ramp it up gradually to 10kV. A common mistake is enabling everything with the supply already set to maximum voltage. This forces the unit to charge rapidly, creating a large inrush current, and it is this current spike, not the voltage itself, that causes components to fail.

Ramping the voltage up safely by hand takes about two minutes to reach 10kV, which can be inconvenient in a fast-paced test environment.

The Heinzinger EVO power supply solves this with a configurable ramping feature. Users can set a voltage rise rate in volts per second, and the supply reaches full voltage automatically over a set period of time, freeing the operator to handle other tasks in the meantime.

title: November 4, 2024 – Just Dirt or the Basis of our Health?
body:
In honor of our recent integration of Medusa Radiometrics into BNC scientific, this week's press release is dedicated to review all things soil health with special regard to agriculture.

California is an agricultural powerhouse – it produces one third of the country's vegetables and one quarter of its fruits and nuts. But as crops are grown and harvested each season, the soil remains the same. What does that mean for soil health?

Topsoil is the basic building block of the foods we eat, and a pivotal part in the cycle of our clean drinking water. It refers to the mixture of sand, silt, clay and organic matter that differs by climate, geolocation, species, and many other factors. It takes healthy topsoil hundreds of years to form and erodes at a much quicker rate. There are many factors that can help alleviate the degradation of topsoil that are important to be wary of as a consumer of agricultural goods.

If topsoil degrades so does the quality of our food. Fertile soil leads to a crop yield that is full of vitamins, minerals, and other nutrients that not only make food tastier but healthier as well. Three targeted actions to boost soil viability include: increasing organic matter such as manure in the soil; creating a structure that ensures plots of land never sit without plant growth; and enacting regenerative agriculture. Aside from providing nutrients, the amount of organic matter in soil increases its ability to retain water. Higher water retention means better water conservation, less nutrient leaching, and less chemical leaching into the groundwater. Cover crops protect the soil from erosion, particularly during harsh rainfall.

Healthy soil is a domino effect of good. Certified organic farmers are responsible for maintaining or improving soil health by attempting to mimic natural processes to foster sustainability. But just like healthy soil has a domino effect, the neglect of soil health starts a chain reaction as well, especially with such large-scale agriculture and quick turnover of land.

Overpumping of groundwater on the central coast has led to seawater intrusion into the aquifers. Excessive buildup of nitrates from decades of fertilizer use and manure means 1 in 10 Californians are exposed to harmful nitrates in their drinking water. Aquifers are drying up, which only means that contaminants are condensing. Drought contributes to plant stress and weakens soil coverage, which then is more prone to erosion via more intense storms brought about by climate change. Considering that about 40% of land in California is used for agriculture, regenerative practices are vital.

The green revolution introduced a few shortcuts to the system, more specifically chemical fertilizers, pesticides, and controlled water supply. The incorporation of these tactics made it possible for farmers to keep up with demand since they present a workaround for less viable land and pest problems. As such, these practices have become deeply ingrained in agriculture even though they come at the expense of the environment. Organic farming does present an alternative, but only 3.97% of California's farms are certified organic. This number stands as a testament to the difficulties of changing entrenched practices, especially when they meet short-term versus long-term goals.

There are many tools available that aid in the process of understanding soil composition in relation to agriculture, industry, other development, weather, or all of the above. Technologies such as these are essential to develop a better understanding of the situations at hand.

title: October 23, 2024 – Nuclear Energy Gives Data Centers Promise for the Future
body:
It's no secret that global internet traffic has been on the rise, and even more remarkably in the years since the pandemic instigated many operations to transition online. A second bump in internet usage followed the introduction of chatbots and the consecutive release of publicly available AI thereafter. And while artificial intelligence shows itself as an ever-promising resource to promote efficiency across industries, there remains one eminent discussion about its heightening utilization: energy consumption.

Artificial intelligence has technically been around for decades. Yet it wasn't until OpenAI's chatbot release in 2022 that demand skyrocketed, and tech responded by introducing a long line of AIs for everything from generative imaging to resume writing. Aside from its most familiar uses, AI has long since proven to be quite advantageous for applications in research, predictive modeling, process creation, and more. According to one study, AI can reduce CO2 emissions by up to 40% when used in smart homes. By having a larger scope of data and faster analysis times, it can streamline operations to cut emissions and costs across all industries. Another example is the EPA's use of AI to detect water pollution violators, which improved detection by 600%. There are endless real-time examples of the benefits of artificial intelligence in conserving resources, which seem to combat its own energy consumption and beg the question: can AI be a net positive?

There's a rush to build more data centers as demand skyrockets. In the US alone, data centers are nearly at their maximum capacity, and the US leads the world in data center numbers. While data centers take up 1% of global energy consumption, it's estimated that AI takes up nearly 20% of data centers' storage capacity. This number has only been growing as AIs become more complex. In turn, electric companies are burdened with balancing the expanding demands of data centers with those of all other existing customers. To mitigate this problem, several notable companies are turning toward nuclear energy: Microsoft, Amazon, and Standard Power, to name a few. Just this last week, Google signed a contract with Kairos to buy electricity from several of their SMRs over the next decade as they are developed. SMRs, or small modular reactors, are gaining traction in particular because of what their name implies: smaller reactors enable placement in less populated areas, and modular designs not only enable quick production times but also future scalability as power needs increase. A significant bonus, as advertised by Kairos, is the passive safety features of SMRs that make them safer alternatives to their traditional counterparts. If SMRs enable data centers to have their own energy source apart from utilities for the general public, the discussion around the resource consumption of artificial intelligence might be nearing a conclusion.

With investments from big tech, it's safe to say that the new age of nuclear energy has begun, and we're along for the ride.

title: September 23, 2024 – Radars: Understanding the Past to Shape the Future (Part III)
body:
Today's radar systems are far more advanced than earlier models. What makes modern radar so powerful is the combination of better electronics, faster processing, and smarter algorithms. These systems can filter out unnecessary data, like trees or mountains, via Kalman filters and focus on what matters, such as fast-moving aircraft or incoming storms.

While radar systems might seem like magic, behind the scenes they rely on finely tuned signals to work properly. This is where vector signal generators (VSGs) come into play. These devices produce highly accurate and complex RF signals that radar systems use for testing and calibration.

Think of a VSG like a conductor in an orchestra: it ensures that all the instruments, or in this case the radar components, are perfectly in sync. Without these signals, a radar system could make mistakes, leading to incorrect readings or even failing to detect an object altogether.

Aside from synchronization, VSGs simulate real-world conditions. They create signals that mimic the kinds of challenges radar systems face, whether it's bad weather, interference from other devices, or objects moving at different speeds. By feeding these simulated signals into the radar system, engineers can make sure it will work correctly in real-life situations.

One of the tools VSGs use is the Pulse Descriptor Word (PDW). A PDW is like a set of instructions the VSG follows to create a radar pulse. It tells the VSG all the important details about the pulse it needs to generate, things like how long the pulse should be, how strong, and how fast it should repeat.

Radar systems send out specific types of pulses to track moving objects. The PDW ensures that the radar sends out the right kind of pulse for each situation, whether it's scanning for a fast-moving jet or a slow-moving ship. These pulses, when reflected, help the radar track movement accurately.

Like any high-tech system, radar needs to be regularly tuned and maintained. Over time, even tiny shifts in the components can lead to errors. Calibration ensures that every part of the radar system is performing exactly as it should, which is especially important in critical fields like aviation and defense, where a minor error can have major consequences.

New technology, like Pulse Calibration Mode (PCM), helps here. Ensuring alignment in a massive radar system is no small task; engineers often spend 12 to 24 hours recalibrating components to ensure the system is accurate. A field-tested PCM feature, created by BNC, allows engineers to perform high-precision calibration for an entire system quickly and effectively, maintaining accuracy in critical parameters like frequency, amplitude, and dynamic power range while cutting calibration time down to roughly two to five minutes.

Modern radar systems are a marvel of engineering, capable of detecting and tracking objects with incredible precision, made possible by tools like vector signal generators and processes like calibration. Innovations like PDW and PCM make it easier than ever to keep radar systems finely tuned, reducing downtime and ensuring reliable performance.

title: September 17, 2024 – Radars: Understanding the Past to Shape the Future (Part II)
body:
In 1842, Christian Andreas Doppler published "Uber das farbige Licht der Doppelsterne" ("On the Colored Light of Double Stars"). As a professor in Prague, Doppler produced over 50 works covering astronomy, mathematics, and physics, but this particular publication would shape the future of countless modern technologies nearly 200 years later. From ultrasounds in medicine to parking sensors, weather prediction in meteorology, and proximity fuses in ordnance, Doppler's work laid the groundwork for innovations we heavily rely on today.

Doppler documented a phenomenon for all kinds of waves: sound, radio frequency (RF), light, gamma rays, and more. He mathematically explained how frequency or wavelength changes depending on the movement of the wave's source and its observer. A simple example is sound waves: think about the noise an ambulance or plane makes as it passes by. You can tell the sound changes as it gets closer and then farther away, even though the plane's engines or the ambulance's siren aren't changing their pitch mid-flight.

That's the Doppler effect in action. When the source of a wave moves toward us, the frequency we experience is higher than when it moves away. This is why the pitch of an approaching siren is initially sharp, then deepens as it passes. The sound waves compress as they move toward you and stretch out as they move away. It's a simple yet powerful example of the Doppler shift, which applies to stationary observers and moving sources.

In modern applications, when both the observer and the source are moving, the foundational Doppler effect equations need adjustment. This adds a layer of complexity, as the system configurations used must adapt to the specific application. A future post will cover how these adjustments apply to modern radar configurations.

title: September 9, 2024 – Radars: Understanding the Past to Shape the Future
body:
At its core, radar is a system that uses radiofrequency (RF) electromagnetic waves to detect objects. The technology, while highly complex in its advanced forms, always revolves around four essential components: a transmitter, an antenna, a receiver, and a signal processing unit.

Here's how it works: the transmitter generates electromagnetic (EM) waves, which are then transmitted through an antenna into space, the atmosphere, or any propagation medium. When these waves encounter an object, whether it's a cloud, a submarine, or a moving vehicle, they reflect back to the radar. The receiver picks up these reflections and sends the data to the signal processing unit, where it determines whether the object is of interest or just clutter. A common civilian example is a speed radar detecting a Doppler shift, a change in frequency caused by a moving car, from which it calculates range and speed.

This post kicks off a deeper dive into radar systems. Future posts will explore the history of radar technology, how it has evolved, and why understanding the physics behind it, such as wavelength, frequency, and phase, is crucial. Later posts will cover attenuation, radar configurations, how different systems interact with the environment, and cutting-edge applications including Pulse Descriptor Word and digital modulation schemes that are powering the next generation of radar technology.

title: August 23, 2024 – Quantum Computing vs Classical Computing
body:
Comparing quantum and classical computing is as similar as a proverbial apples and oranges comparison.

At the very heart of classical computers are these facts: they are able to store data, they require human instruction via programming to work accurately and fast, they do not have intelligence of their own, and they do not possess the power to learn.

Classical computers have many unique qualities, however the divide between them shows when considering that a classical computer with N bits performs a maximum of N calculations simultaneously, while quantum computers perform up to 2^N calculations. Translated: if a classical processor yields 10 calculations, the quantum processor in comparison will manage 2^10, or 1,024 calculations.

Classical computing as we know it will not go away. However, as quantum computing continues to take hold, it has the power to be a game changer across many industries.

Quantum computing relies on quantum bits (qubits) instead of the ones and zeros of classical bits. To perform a computation with many qubits, they are sustained in a quantum-coherent state, whereby qubits are entangled and where a tweak to one qubit may influence all of them. Performing computational operations while adding extra qubits can potentially double the resources of a quantum computer.

Fifty qubits has long been considered the approximate number at which quantum computing becomes capable of calculations that would take too long via classical machines. Quantum computers must deal with noise that rapidly derails calculations, and errors in the form of noise, faults, and loss of quantum coherence are crippling to their operation. All qubits must be kept coherent, which is very difficult, and quantum computers need to be kept at temperatures close to absolute zero.

Performing classical computations is quite simple: an input goes in, an algorithm processes it, and an output occurs. Quantum computations, however, rely on a range of different inputs and return a range of possibilities. There is no straightforward answer, only an estimate of the probability of different answers.

There's no doubt that quantum computing will transform many industries, though those changes will take time. According to a 2020 McKinsey report, "A Game Plan for Quantum Computing," the estimate is that by 2030 only 2,000 to 5,000 quantum computers will be operational, and the hardware and software needed to handle the most complex problems may not exist until 2035 or beyond. In the meantime, researchers access quantum computers through cloud services such as those offered by Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure.

Classical computers will not go away since we will always need the direct answers they provide. Quantum computers, however, will be adopted over time as huge investments continue to produce results, dependent on their ability to provide enormous computational capacity for complex problems with different input variables and complex algorithms.

What is important isn't the comparison of the inherent characteristics of apples and oranges, but leveraging the attributes of both types of computing, classical and quantum, to unlock quantum's full power and potential.

This excerpt is adapted from "QC 01 - The Nuts and Bolts (and Qubits) of Quantum Computing," a course offered by BNC Academy.

title: August 7, 2024 – The Necessity of Radar in Fighting Megafires
body:
Here on the west coast, we've experienced multiple of the deadliest fires on state record in the past half-decade alone. Drought, heat waves, and high winds have permanently hammered their way into weather forecasts.

The megafires that continue to torment the west have defied known fire behavior and diminished the efficiency of age-old fire fighting tactics. To regain footing, technology and data acquisition is vital. Radar is one such tool that has already proved its worth in predicting, detecting, and fighting fires, and its evolution is critical to lessen the threat of such devastation.

High winds, dry air, and high temperatures present the ideal environment for fires to trigger and grow. Drought has dried out trees and made even the most fire-resistant trees vulnerable, and nights have warmed considerably along with a substantial loss in coastal fog. The fuel is there and ready to burn, so reliable weather forecasts are more pertinent than ever to ensure the correct preparations are taken from an individual to a national level.

Most wildfires are caused by human activity, and precautionary measures such as campfire restrictions, limited road access near flammable fuels or high winds, and power shutoffs are already in place. Still, several major approaches remain: cracking down on regulations, and beefing up fire-fighting tactics and tools to maintain a front against the behavior of megafires.

Understanding weather, climate, terrain, and fuel sources dictates evacuations, front-line management, and fire growth predictions. A combination of weather radar, satellite imagery, drones, and infrared mapping make up the tool belt that's become necessary for wildfire management. Real-time monitoring combined with models developed from known fire behavior, flammability of vegetation, and terrain helps predict fire behavior, though these models can become outdated or inaccurate as fires grow more unpredictable.

Weather forecasting is now quicker, more accurate, and can provide more advanced readings. A state-of-the-art weather radar developed by a team at Oklahoma University utilizes phased array radar, which has a much larger scope than Doppler radar. Since lightning strikes are a leading cause of wildfires next to human activity, improved weather forecasting helps ensure that resources are at the ready.

Radar is also used to study the fires themselves. A team at San Jose State University developed a portable radar system that has shed light on fire behavior, using a wavelength that provides a more detailed view of the inner workings of fires than Doppler radar.

Arbitrary waveform generators, RF/microwave signal generators, and RF power sensors are several technologies in the realm of radar that have seen steady advancements. AWGs have reached a level of innovation where some models can be used for radar applications, while RF/microwave signal sources and RF power sensors are traditionally used for radar, with a wide variety of equipment available for different niche specifications.

title: July 29, 2024 – Radiation: What You Should Know
body:
UV rays, old televisions, smoke detectors, granite countertops, and x-rays all have one thing in common: they're all radioactive to a certain degree. Radiation is everywhere, but thanks to science and strict monitoring there are ways to figure out when concern is warranted. Becoming familiar with the classifications of radiation, ionizing and non-ionizing, is the first step in remaining safe.

Ionizing radiation, otherwise known as nuclear radiation, has high enough energy to ionize molecules and cause biological damage. Common sources include UV rays, cosmic particles, radon gas, medical imaging, smoke detectors, potassium-enriched fertilizers, food sterilization methods, and forms of technology that utilize radionuclides within professional environments. Other natural sources that emit doses too low to cause harm are called background radiation.

The average person not working with radioactive material typically absorbs a background dose of 0.1 to 0.2 rem per year.

Non-ionizing radiation is the second classification and is generally considered harmless because its photon energy or intensity is so low. Radio and TV waves, cell phones, and microwaves fall into this category. Ongoing studies of exposure to electromagnetic radiation produced by mobile phones and other technology suggest a possible correlation between long-term exposure and weakened immune response, though results remain inconclusive. The public can keep up to date with findings through the EPA's RadTown radiation education website.

Our bodies have mechanisms to reverse the effects of radiation, but damage is cumulative as these mechanisms weaken over time. This is why it's important to remain aware of radiation sources and learn what can be done to minimize risk. Radon gas poisoning, for example, is a leading cause of lung cancer yet can easily be measured with a RAD device and prevented by ensuring a building is properly sealed and ventilated.

Even under heavy precautions, accidents happen. Hazmat teams and first responders carry radiation detection devices for use when there is a spill or other type of disaster, and security personnel typically utilize RIIDs to ensure that arenas or other large public event spaces are clear of dangers.

title: July 22, 2024 – A Closer Look at MRI

title: May 30, 2024 – Why is Afterglow Important in Scintillation?
body:
One property of scintillation is afterglow, defined as the fraction of scintillation light still present for a certain time after the radiation energy, including gamma ray or x-ray excitation, stops. When a scintillator detects incoming radiation, depending on the quality of the crystal material, the radiation's charged particles can be trapped in impurities or structural crystal defects. This is what causes the afterglow effect in a variety of scintillators, and manufacturers of scintillation materials aim to reduce this excess.

In several medical imaging applications such as PET, afterglow must be reduced to prevent energy resolution degradation. PET imaging and other high-energy physics applications require rapid response and precise measurements, and afterglow can reduce the quality of measurements achieved.

The afterglow effect can last for several minutes after the initial measurement, influencing the scintillation properties. To preserve the sensitivity and accuracy of radiation measurement, it's important to reduce afterglow in detection.

There are many materials BNC offers that provide low afterglow, notably LYSO, BGO, and LaBr. LYSO is often the best choice for PET medical imaging because of its higher light output and lower afterglow compared with BGO.

The crystal growth process and purification of materials can help reduce afterglow. Scintillators can also undergo codoping to reduce afterglow, though this process can affect other scintillation properties like energy resolution and light yield. title: May 13, 2024 – Neutron Detectors and Their Performance
body:
The detection of neutrons requires a special environment because neutrons do not typically cause ionization, since they are not charged particles. Detecting neutrons requires an environment of high neutron cross-section nuclides (target). Nuclides commonly used for neutron detectors are helium-3 (³He), lithium-6 (⁶Li), boron-10 (¹⁰B) and uranium-235 (²³⁵U). The detector material is surrounded by a moderator, which reduces the kinetic energy of the neutron (slows it down). Moderated neutrons are commonly called thermal neutrons, which provide a high probability of interaction with the target material. The following are the most common neutron detector types used today.

The ³He Gas-Filled Proportional Detector

Since ³He has no electrical charge, neutron interactions with atomic electrons are impossible, unlike in X-ray, gamma, electron, or beta detectors. Instead, neutrons rely on an abundance of atomic nuclei with high neutron cross-section. ³He is an efficient neutron detector because it absorbs thermal neutrons and produces a proton and a ³H ion, with negligible sensitivity to gamma rays. Its supply is limited, however, since it is a byproduct of tritium decay, and tritium itself is produced either as part of the weapons program or as a byproduct of reactor operation. This limited availability keeps the price of ³He detectors relatively high.

Lithium-6 (⁶Li) Neutron Detector

These detectors combine ⁶Li and cerium ions into a scintillating glass fiber composition. ⁶Li has a high cross section for thermal neutron absorption, producing a tritium ion, an alpha particle, and kinetic energy, which transfers to the cerium ions and produces a flash of light with several thousand photons for each neutron absorbed. This reaction yields pulses much larger than the ³He reaction. The glass fiber acts as a wave guide for the scintillation light, coupled to a PMT, and pulse shape discrimination further enhances the separation of gamma and neutron events.

The CLYC and CLLBC Neutron Detector

CLYC (Cs2LiYCl6:Ce) and CLLBC (Cs2LiLa[Br,Cl]6:Ce) detectors have similar reactions with lithium as described above. What makes them unique is that the same detector offers both gamma spectroscopy and neutron detection, with good gamma resolution and neutron separation at the same time. These dual-mode detectors are readily available in 2x2 inch sizes and larger.

Boron Trifluoride and Boron Nitride Neutron Detectors

This detector uses ionization to detect neutrons much like the ³He detector, but uses boron trifluoride (BF3) gas as the detecting medium instead. The boron-10 isotope in the gas is a good neutron absorber, and this detector is also highly sensitive. The boron nitride (BN) detector can detect fast neutrons without a moderator, and can be produced in large sheets for power plants and other nuclear facilities.

The Domino Neutron Detector

The Domino uses semiconductor technology to form tiles backfilled with ⁶LiF or ¹⁰B, known as Microstructured Semiconductor Neutron Detectors (MSND). This gives a reduced form factor with the flexibility to stack or configure tiles into different shapes, with a high gamma rejection ratio.

The Rem Ball

This device measures neutron dose equivalent. It takes the form of a large ball incorporating a moderator, and is generally large and stationary. Measuring neutron dose or dose rate is complex and cannot be accomplished with any of the previously discussed detector types.

Each of these detectors has its own advantages and disadvantages, so the right choice depends on the specific application and form factor needed. Please consult with BNC to determine the correct detector and configuration for your specific need.

title: April 22, 2024 – Comparing LBC and LaBr3:Ce Scintillators: A Detailed Overview
body:
Lanthanum BromoChloride (LBC) scintillators, represented by the chemical formula LaBr2.85Cl0.15:Ce, are gaining prominence in radiation detection due to features that closely align with those of the well known LaBr3:Ce crystals. These scintillators are valued for their high-resolution capabilities and enhanced mechanical robustness, making them an attractive alternative in scientific and industrial applications.

Key Properties of Lanthanum BromoChloride

LBC scintillators deliver energy resolutions of approximately 3% Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) at 662 keV, similar to the performance of LaBr3:Ce crystals. This level of resolution is essential for precise gamma-ray spectrometry, important in fields such as medical imaging and environmental monitoring. Despite these similarities, LBC scintillators offer improved mechanical strength over LaBr3:Ce, making LBC more suitable for applications where physical robustness matters as much as detection precision, such as portable radiation detectors used in harsh environments.

Drawbacks in Comparison to LaBr3:Ce

A notable disadvantage of both LBC and LaBr3:Ce scintillators is their susceptibility to background noise from La-138, which can interfere with the clarity of radiation detection. This is a shared limitation, so it does not diminish LBC's comparative advantage in other areas.

Applications Reflecting Their Comparative Strengths

The enhanced mechanical strength and high-resolution capabilities of LBC make it useful not only in typical environments where LaBr3:Ce is used, but also in more demanding settings, such as geological surveying and outdoor environmental monitoring, where equipment may be exposed to mechanical stress.

title: March 1, 2024 – SiPM Readout Method to Improve Scintillation Performance
body:
Berkeley Nucleonics offers Silicon Photomultiplier Tubes (SiPMs) as a light read-out method for scintillators. Unlike traditional photomultiplier tubes (PMTs), SiPMs behave quite differently in spectroscopic performance. SiPM elements work best where small size and low voltage (20V-30V) are required, and are typically arranged in matrices of 6x6, 3x3, or 4x4 mm. They are mechanically compact and insensitive to magnetic fields.

SiPMs can be coupled with a variety of detector materials, including plastic, liquid, and inorganic materials such as CeBr3 and YAP:Ce. With plastic detectors such as EJ-440, the SiPM can be optically coupled to a built-in amplifier that allows the signal to be analyzed. SiPMs are also used in pixelated detectors, where higher quantities of scintillation crystals are arranged in a grid to help detect the intensity of radiation and provide spatial insight.

The placement and arrangement of the SiPMs often impacts crystal performance directly. For large scintillation crystals, the SiPMs must be as few as possible and carefully placed to reduce capacitive noise on the signal; too many SiPMs on a large surface area can degrade energy resolution and increase capacitive noise.

All SiPM-based detectors are intended for use at room temperature. Cooling SiPM electronics below 60°C can damage the material, and while shielding can be used to protect the electronics from temperature effects, this approach is not recommended. Radiation in the environment, such as high neutron flux, can also reduce SiPM quality, so it is important to consider radiation type, energy level, and temperature in the operating environment.

title: February 26, 2024 – The Complete Guide to Vector Network Analyzers
body:
In the intricate world of electrical engineering, precise measurement tools are paramount for the development, testing, and optimization of radio frequency (RF) and microwave circuits. One indispensable instrument is the Vector Network Analyzer (VNA), a cornerstone in the analysis of network parameters, offering detailed insight into the performance characteristics of RF components.

What is a Vector Network Analyzer?

A Vector Network Analyzer is an advanced test instrument that measures the complex impedance, phase, and magnitude of RF signals. Unlike its scalar counterpart, which only measures magnitude, the VNA provides a vector (magnitude and phase) analysis, enabling engineers to fully characterize RF components and systems.

Key Features of VNAs

Frequency range is a defining characteristic of any VNA, determining the spectrum over which the device can perform measurements.

S-parameters, or scattering parameters, are the core of VNA measurements. They describe how RF energy scatters or reflects from a network under test, giving insight into how a device behaves under different conditions and helping engineers optimize its performance.

Dynamic range indicates the range over which a VNA can accurately measure signal reflection and transmission. A high dynamic range allows measurement of both very strong and very weak signals, which is important for analyzing devices with high return losses or very low signal transmission.

Applications of Vector Network Analyzers

  • Telecommunications: antenna design, cable and connector characterization, and wireless system development
  • Semiconductor manufacturing: testing components such as amplifiers and mixers
  • Material analysis: characterizing the dielectric properties of materials at different frequencies
  • Education and research: teaching tools for RF principles and for research in universities and laboratories

How Does a VNA Work?

The basic operating principle of a VNA involves generating a known RF signal, which is transmitted through the device under test (DUT). The VNA measures the reflected and transmitted signals, analyzing their magnitude and phase relative to the input signal, allowing it to calculate the S-parameters and provide a comprehensive view of the DUT's characteristics.

title: February 20, 2024 – Unveiling the Strengths of LaBr3 for Gamma-Ray Spectroscopy in Harsh Environments
body:
In the world of nuclear physics and radiation detection, the quest for materials that can perform under extreme conditions is relentless. Gamma-ray spectroscopy, a technique pivotal for identifying radioactive isotopes and analyzing nuclear reactions, demands detectors that are not only highly efficient but also resilient. Lanthanum Bromide (LaBr3) has emerged as a material of choice, particularly for applications requiring precise measurements in harsh environments.

High resolution: the keystone of LaBr3

At the heart of LaBr3's superiority is its outstanding energy resolution. Energy resolution is a critical parameter in gamma-ray spectroscopy, as it determines the detector's ability to distinguish between gamma rays of closely spaced energies. LaBr3 scintillators exhibit energy resolutions significantly better than those of traditional materials, such as sodium iodide (NaI) or even cesium iodide (CsI). This heightened resolution is primarily attributed to LaBr3's high light output, which is about three times higher than that of NaI(Tl).

Characteristics of lanthanum bromide scintillators

  • Photoelectron yield (relative to NaI(Tl) for gamma rays): 165%
  • Energy resolution at 662 keV: 2.6%
  • Temperature range: -30 to 60 degrees C
  • Emission peak wavelength: 380 nm
  • Initial decay time: 0.016 microseconds
  • Material density: 5.08 g/cm3
  • Hygroscopic: yes

Speed of response: capturing fast events

The temporal resolution, or the speed at which a detector can process radiation events, is another domain where LaBr3 excels. The material's decay time is on the order of 16 nanoseconds, considerably faster than many other scintillators. This rapid response enables LaBr3-based detectors to accurately record events in high-flux environments, such as those found near reactors or in space.

Robustness in harsh conditions

Harsh environments pose a spectrum of challenges for radiation detectors, from extreme temperatures to high levels of background radiation. LaBr3's chemical and physical properties afford it a robustness that is essential for such conditions. Unlike some other scintillators, LaBr3 is relatively insensitive to temperature fluctuations, maintaining its performance over a wide temperature range.

Versatility and ease of integration

The adaptability of LaBr3 to different detection configurations adds to its appeal. Its scintillators can be produced in various shapes and sizes, catering to a wide range of spectroscopic applications, from portable radiation detectors to airborne surveys and fixed monitoring stations. title: January 11, 2024 – Neutron Detection Across Energy Ranges
body:
To determine which scintillation material is best for an application, it is crucial to know the energy range needed for detection. This holds true for all types of radiation, including gamma, beta, and alpha, and is especially important for neutron detection.

A different type of scintillator and size may be recommended for detecting high-energy, fast neutrons versus lower-energy neutrons. CLYC:Ce detectors, a newer inorganic material, have a lower cross section for neutrons, meaning the material becomes less effective at higher neutron energies, and is well suited to gamma/neutron separation at lower neutron energies.

CLYC:Ce detectors also provide a strong solution when an application requires good energy resolution for gamma radiation. Gamma and neutron events can be differentiated through pulse shape discrimination, by measuring the thermal neutron peak between 3.1 and 3.2 MeV. With a high light yield of 20,000 photons/MeV and a high density of 3.3 g/cm3, CLYC:Ce is suitable for a variety of applications.

Any inorganic material can detect neutrons via elastic and inelastic scattering, but for high energies, the better approach is to use a liquid scintillator and digitize the signals. Liquid scintillators are organic solutions that can be encapsulated in a variety of geometries and read out with a suitable PMT. One consideration for liquid scintillators is the flammability of the material; if the material is flammable, the liquid cell is classified as a dangerous good, as is the case with EJ-315.

Berkeley Nucleonics offers liquid scintillator cells such as EJ-309 and EJ-301, which are not classified as dangerous goods. title: January 10, 2024 – Understanding the Differences: RF Signal Generators vs. RF Synthesizers
body:
In the realm of radiofrequency (RF) technology, signal creation is fundamental. Two key instruments used in this domain are RF signal generators and RF synthesizers. Though they share the common goal of producing RF signals, the methodologies and applications of these tools differ significantly.

What is an RF signal generator?

An RF signal generator is a versatile and precise instrument used in the testing, design, and maintenance of radio frequency equipment and systems. It is capable of generating continuous wave signals at a set frequency, and its hallmark is the extensive control it provides over signal parameters such as frequency, amplitude, and modulation.

What is an RF synthesizer?

An RF synthesizer is a type of signal generator that creates RF signals through a combination of frequency multipliers, dividers, and internal circuitry. The focus is on synthesizing a frequency that closely approximates the desired output, with the ability to quickly switch between frequencies for applications requiring rapid frequency changes.

Comparing the two

RF signal generators are often used in RF research, equipment design, and calibration. They are preferred in scenarios where signal integrity and precision are paramount, such as in laboratory settings or complex system diagnostics. RF synthesizers, on the other hand, find their use in more dynamic environments, such as telecommunications, where the ability to rapidly switch frequencies matters more than the absolute precision of each signal.

Choosing the right instrument depends on the specific needs of an RF application. For precision and meticulous control, an RF signal generator is ideal; for adaptability and swift frequency switching, an RF synthesizer fits the bill. Berkeley Nucleonics offers a comprehensive selection of both; learn more in the RF and microwave signal generators line.
