title: November 30, 2023 – RF/Microwave-to-Optics Generation and Conversion
body:
RF/microwave-to-optics generation is emerging as a leading approach for the next generation of quantum technology. As industry and academia look for ways to scale quantum computers and quantum networks, microwave-to-optics conversion has become a common theme across research papers and journals. Physical optics platforms used to obtain coherent millimeter-wave frequencies include atoms, lasers, metamaterials, and other optical methods.

Many RF/microwave-to-optics conversion systems share a similar structure. The signal source is produced by an RF generator using a continuous wave (CW), pulsed signal, chirp, or similar waveform. These signal generator functions are available in the multi-channel Vector Signal Generator Model 875 and across Berkeley Nucleonics' RF and microwave signal generator series. Effective microwave-to-optic transduction depends on a low-phase-noise RF signal generator to produce optical millimeter-wave signals at the output of the optical system.

The RF signal enters a cavity, which functions like an RF mixer, converting RF/microwave frequencies to terahertz (THz) frequencies. At the same time, an external higher-frequency source is combined into the cavity, similar to a local oscillator (LO), carrying frequencies beyond the initial RF signal source to drive the RF-to-optics conversion. The cavity then produces multiple output signal channels across a range of optical frequencies.

Building on these techniques, along with multi-channel conversion and amplitude control of frequency channels, quantum technology can advance further. Solid-state qubits are central to quantum information processing because of their ability to encode and manipulate quantum information with enhanced stability and coherence, opening research directions across optics, photonics, lasers, 5G, and potentially 6G communications.

In 5G and 6G telecommunications, optical fibers offer high bandwidth and low signal loss, making them well suited to transmitting high-frequency microwave signals over long distances. Synchronization is critical in 5G/6G networks for coordinated communication between base stations, and microwave-to-optics conversion can be used to distribute precise timing signals over optical fiber networks to support that synchronization.

While 5G is focused on classical telecommunication, 6G is expected to explore quantum communication and THz frequency bands. Microwave-to-optics conversion can support quantum communication systems that interface with quantum devices and networks, and can be adapted to handle THz signals as part of broader millimeter-wave communication infrastructure.

title: October 24, 2023 – Scintillation Detectors: Attenuation Length of Optical Emission
body:
One important aspect of scintillation is how bright the fluorescence is after detecting radiation. Attenuation length, or absorption rate, in scintillators is defined as the distance light must travel to be reduced to 1/e (37%) of its original intensity. This is a concern for users, as attenuation or absorption in the scintillation material can hinder research conclusions and radiation detection. Berkeley Nucleonics does not publish a single standard attenuation length for its scintillators because of the many external factors that influence it: the size of the scintillator, the energy range measured, and material density all play a role.

For each scintillation material, Berkeley Nucleonics guarantees a set energy resolution, and optical attenuation length is generally reflected within that parameter. Please refer to Berkeley Nucleonics product datasheets for specific figures.

title: August 22, 2023 – Radar Signal Simulation (PDW / EW) | Model 875 Vector Signal Generator
body:
Understanding radar signal simulation

Radar system simulation is a method to test the detection capabilities of aircraft, ships, submarines, and land vehicles against hostile threats. The process involves creating a virtual environment where the interactions between radar signals and various targets are modeled, including the creation, transmission, propagation, and reception of radar signals. Its primary goal is to generate realistic radar signals that can be used for testing signal processing algorithms, evaluating radar performance, and training radar operators.

How radar signal simulation works

Radar signal simulation combines knowledge from radar theory, electromagnetic wave propagation, signal processing, and target modeling to create a theoretical representation of radar operations, modeling factors such as signal modulation, pulse repetition frequency, pulse width, carrier frequency, Doppler effects, and noise interference. Specific environments need to be emulated for precise measurements, including free-field anechoic chambers, maritime environments (accounting for sea clutter, wave reflections, and varying sea states), and aerial or mountainous terrain (accounting for atmospheric conditions and free-space propagation).

Pulse Descriptor Word (PDW) is also an important measurement parameter in radar signal simulation, condensing radar pulses into a single data packet through digital techniques.

Vector signal generators in radar signal simulation

Vector signal generators (VSGs) are used to simulate radar signals for testing and evaluating the performance of electronic countermeasures (ECM) and electronic support measures (ESM) systems, valued for their versatility, precision, and ability to generate complex, modulated signals.

  • Signal realization: VSGs generate custom waveforms that closely mimic real-world EW radar conditions, varying in amplitude, frequency, phase, and modulation
  • Modulation and dynamic scenarios: VSGs can replicate modulation schemes such as AM, FM, and PM, and account for dynamic scenarios involving moving targets and Doppler shifts
  • Phase coherence: VSGs with multi-channel capabilities maintain precise phase synchronization between channels, important for simulating phased-array radar setups

VSGs help radar engineers, researchers, and operators assess EW radar systems under diverse conditions, including scenarios involving PDWs. The Model 875 by Berkeley Nucleonics is built to support this kind of radar signal simulation work.

Understanding MIMO wireless technology

Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) is a wireless communication technique that uses multiple antennas at both the transmitter and receiver to improve data throughput, signal quality, and overall system performance, taking advantage of the spatial dimension to increase the capacity and reliability of wireless communication systems.

How MIMO works

MIMO operates on the principle of multipath propagation, where signals take multiple paths to reach the receiver due to reflections, diffractions, and scattering. MIMO systems exploit these multiple paths to transmit multiple data streams simultaneously, providing spatial multiplexing (increasing data rate and spectral efficiency), diversity gain (mitigating fading and interference through redundancy), interference reduction, and beamforming (precise control of signal directionality).

title: July 3, 2023 – Advancements in Technology, Aided by Lanthanides
body:
This post responds to "The Role of Lanthanide Luminescence in Advancing Technology," published in RSC Advances by Gabriella Tessitore, Gabrielle A. Mandl, Steven L. Maurizio, Mannu Kaur, and John A. Capobianco. The authors trace lanthanides' role from initial discovery through current and prospective innovations.

The discovery of lanthanide luminescence has been vital to technological advancement since its first application in lighting displays. Lanthanide discovery predated technological use by nearly two centuries, and extraction difficulties, combined with similarities between elements, complicated progress and established high costs that persist today.

Phosphor necessity emerged with the 1927 invention of the first fluorescent light. Phosphors were essential to counteracting the UV-emissive chromaticity of metal vapor to generate appropriate light color. The first commercial lanthanide-based phosphor appeared in 1965, when YVO4:Eu3+ was used in CRT-based color television, completing the red-green-blue principle. CRT displays have since been phased out except for some marine and aviation applications.

Light-emitting diodes, and later hybrid organic-LED technology, have replaced CRTs. LEDs produce light by pumping electrical current into semiconductor materials, converting electrical energy into luminescence. While lanthanides have served as dopants for blue-light LEDs, their use in OLED technology remains largely undeveloped despite promising applications.

Current Applications

Lanthanides have enabled major advances in laser technology affecting numerous industries.

Lanthanide-based scintillator materials rank among the highest-performing commercial materials available, largely due to four properties: light yield, emission wavelength, energy resolution, and decay time. Scintillators are essential for image-based inspection and radiation detectors and play a major role in national security, enabling radiation and radioisotope identification and detection (RIID). Berkeley Nucleonics uses LaBr3:Ce3+ and CeBr3 in commercial RIID devices. Further advances toward compact, single-material personal RIID detectors for combined gamma and neutron detection began with CLYC in 2014; in 2017, BNC and other companies began producing CLLBC, which demonstrates a much higher light yield than CLYC.

Additional scintillator applications include well-logging in the oil and natural gas industries, which demand compact, rugged materials able to withstand harsh temperatures and vibration. NaI(Tl) was the primary option through the 1980s; lanthanide-based detectors are now under consideration for future development in this space.

Lanthanides have contributed to societal advancement, from pivotal technologies to more everyday applications. After nearly half a century of development, lanthanide-based solar technologies show promising potential for advancing green energy.

Adapted from: "The Role of Lanthanide Luminescence in Advancing Technology" by Gabriella Tessitore, Gabrielle A. Mandl, Steven L. Maurizio, Mannu Kaur, and John A. Capobianco, RSC Advances.

title: June 12, 2023 – Scintillator | What are Scintillator Materials?
body:
Scintillators are luminescent materials that emit light when exposed to ionizing radiation. They have transformed the field of radiation detection and imaging and play a vital role in applications ranging from homeland security to medical diagnostics.

Properties and Mechanism

Scintillators possess the property of luminescence, which allows them to absorb energy from incoming particles and re-emit it as light. When struck by ionizing radiation, a scintillator absorbs the energy and enters an excited state, and the subsequent relaxation process can produce either delayed fluorescence or phosphorescence, depending on the type of transition and the wavelength of the emitted photon.

Applications

  • Homeland security: used extensively as radiation detectors to help identify and prevent the illicit transport of radioactive materials
  • Particle detectors: in high-energy physics, aiding in the detection and characterization of subatomic particles produced in accelerators and colliders

title: June 7, 2023 – Multichannel Signal Generators and Local Oscillators
body:
In radio frequency (RF) systems, the generation and manipulation of signals plays a crucial role in applications such as wireless communications, radar systems, and electronic warfare. RF mixers are key components that enable the frequency translation and signal processing these applications require, and multichannel signal generators and local oscillators are fundamental building blocks of RF mixers, providing the signals needed for mixing operations.

Multichannel Signal Generators

Multichannel signal generators produce multiple signals simultaneously, each with different characteristics such as frequency, phase, and amplitude, often implemented using direct digital synthesis (DDS), in which a digital-to-analog converter is driven by a high-speed digital clock and controlled by a microprocessor or FPGA. Modern units offer real-time control of individual channels, allowing rapid changes in frequency, modulation scheme, and phase relationship, versatility that is especially useful in software-defined radios (SDRs). Applications include frequency conversion, signal synthesis for testing and calibration, and waveform generation for modulated signals throughout the development, prototyping, and testing of RF systems.

Local Oscillators

Local oscillators (LOs) are essential components in RF mixers, providing the frequency reference for mixing operations: a stable, accurate signal at a specific frequency that combines with the input signal to produce the desired output frequency. LOs can be implemented using voltage-controlled oscillators (VCOs), phase-locked loops (PLLs), and frequency synthesizers. Phase noise is a critical parameter affecting overall signal quality and system performance, and LOs with wide frequency agility are in high demand, enabling agile frequency hopping, fast channel switching, and multi-band operation without physical component changes.

Applications of LOs in RF mixers include frequency upconversion and downconversion, heterodyne receivers, and frequency modulation, used in wireless transceivers, radar systems, and satellite communication equipment. title: May 17, 2023 – Noise-Parameter-Measurement Method
body:
Noise Parameters

A noise factor (or equivalently a noise figure) of a device is a common metric for representing the amount of signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) degradation due to noise generated by the device. While noise factors are commonly used, they are not invariant quantities of the associated devices and are affected by how the devices are embedded into larger systems. To model this dependence, noise parameters are used: minimum noise factor (Fmin), equivalent noise resistance (Rn), and optimal signal-source admittance for minimum noise (Yopt).

Measurement of noise parameters involves driving the device with a few signal sources having different admittances, determining the noise factor for each, and then solving for the four noise parameters using these results. A selection of well-placed admittance values, rather than a large number chosen for high redundancy, is desirable to reduce measurement time while maintaining adequate accuracy.

Earlier work investigated uniform coverage of source admittances within the Smith chart but did not show theoretically why the proposed patterns were optimum. Later work described a non-uniform pattern by augmenting that earlier pattern with extra admittances, demonstrating stronger performance. A further study performed a theoretical analysis of the system of equations solved to extract the noise parameters, showing that four Smith-chart regions of admittance values guarantee a diagonally dominant system of equations and thus guarantee a solution. NoiseTech identified the flexibility and performance of this four-region method as key to its line of impedance generators.

Experimental Comparison of Measurement Methods

The goal of the experimental work was to demonstrate that the proposed 4-point admittance selection method extracts the same noise parameters, within measurement uncertainty, as other established admittance patterns, and that it can measure noise parameters in cases where other methods cannot.

Several amplifiers were measured with five different admittance methods, including the proposed 4-point method, an earlier 4-point method, a 5-point cross method, a 2-step nine-point method, and a random 30-point method. Noise parameters for methods with more than four measurements were determined using a least-squares method, while direct solutions were possible with the two 4-point methods.

The noise parameters for the measured devices fell within the measurement uncertainties of the other methods, demonstrating agreement across all five approaches. Measurements also showed that source admittances at the low and high ends of the range can drastically increase noise parameter uncertainty, with uncertainty generally minimized in the middle of the range.

Wideband Measurements

Additional measurements demonstrated the flexibility of the proposed 4-point pattern in cases where a mechanical tuner could not produce a full set of admittances at lower frequencies. The proposed method was able to adjust its diagonal-dominant regions, allowing extraction of noise parameters beyond what would be possible with the mechanical tuner alone, producing mean noise parameter values close to a least-squares solution using all available admittances.

Advantages of the Approach

Minimizing the number of source admittance measurements needed for accurate noise parameter determination reduces measurement time and simplifies the procedure. The proposed 4-point method does not require a least-squares solution because it is not over-determined like other methods, and its pattern-selection procedure allows scale factors to be changed to modify the size and position of admittance regions while still meeting diagonal dominance requirements. NoiseTech impedance generators are designed to produce sets of signal-source admittances that remain within the required regions over a wide frequency range, allowing wideband noise parameter measurements with low uncertainty.

title: May 5th, 2023 – From Crystal Growth to Assembly: The Manufacturing Process of Custom Nal Scintillation Crystals
body:
Scintillation crystals are used in a wide range of applications, from medical imaging to nuclear physics research. Among the most commonly used scintillation materials is sodium iodide (NaI), which is widely used due to its high light yield, good energy resolution, and low cost. This article provides an overview of the manufacturing process for custom NaI scintillation crystals.

Materials Used

The main materials used in the manufacture of NaI scintillation crystals are sodium iodide (NaI) and thallium (Tl). NaI is a hygroscopic material that can easily absorb moisture from the environment, which can reduce scintillation efficiency. Thallium is added to the NaI crystal to improve its scintillation properties.

Manufacturing Process

The manufacturing process for NaI scintillation crystals involves several steps: crystal growth, cutting and polishing, and assembly.

Crystal Growth

The first step is to grow the NaI crystal, typically using the Bridgman-Stockbarger method. A seed crystal of NaI is placed in a high-temperature furnace along with a charge of NaI and Tl. The furnace is heated to a high temperature, causing the NaI and Tl to melt, and the seed crystal is then slowly pulled through the molten mixture, allowing a crystal to grow from the seed.

Cutting and Polishing

Once grown, the crystal is cut and polished to the desired size and shape, typically using diamond saws and progressively finer polishing wheels until a smooth surface is achieved. The surface of the crystal is critical to its scintillation properties, since any imperfections can reduce efficiency.

Assembly

The final step is to assemble the crystal into a scintillation detector, typically mounting it onto a photomultiplier tube (PMT) or other light detector, which converts the light produced by the crystal into an electrical signal. The crystal is typically surrounded by a reflector material, such as aluminum or magnesium oxide, to improve light collection efficiency.

Technical Specifications

The performance of a NaI scintillation crystal is characterized by light output, energy resolution, and decay time. If you need a custom NaI scintillation crystal for your project, please fill out the questionnaire here.

title: April 26, 2023 – The Power of Vector Signal Generators in Modern Communication Systems
body:
In modern communication systems, the demand for accurate and versatile signal generation has increased significantly. Vector signal generators (VSGs) are a crucial tool used in the development, testing, and validation of communication systems.

What is a Vector Signal Generator?

A vector signal generator (VSG) is a test and measurement instrument used to generate and modulate radio-frequency (RF) signals. VSGs are capable of generating a wide range of modulated signals, including amplitude modulation (AM), frequency modulation (FM), phase modulation (PM), and more advanced digital modulation schemes such as quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) and orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM).

How Does a Vector Signal Generator Work?

A VSG produces RF signals by generating baseband signals and modulating them with an RF carrier. The baseband signals are generated using arbitrary waveform generators (AWGs) that produce digital waveforms. These waveforms are then converted to analog signals using digital-to-analog converters (DACs). The analog signals are fed into a modulator that modulates the RF carrier with the baseband signal, producing an RF signal.

Applications of Vector Signal Generators

  • Arbitrary I/Q waveform: VSGs can generate complex I/Q (in-phase and quadrature) modulated signals used in advanced communication systems such as 5G and Wi-Fi, which require precise timing, frequency, and phase control
  • Radar signal simulation: used to simulate radar signals for testing and validation of radar systems, which require accurate frequency, phase, and amplitude control
  • Receiver testing: used to test the performance of radio receivers by producing a signal that simulates a transmitter, then analyzing the receiver's output
  • Avionic modulation emulation: used to emulate avionic modulation schemes, such as those used in military and commercial aircraft communication systems

One of the key advantages of the PVX-4110 is its ability to produce high-voltage pulses with fast rise times and short pulse widths, useful for the electrostatic modulation of particle beams, where precise timing and control are critical for accurate results.

A common application is in time-of-flight mass spectrometry, where it drives the extraction grids that release ions from the ion source and accelerate them toward the detector. By pulsing the extraction grids at specific intervals, researchers can separate ions with different mass-to-charge ratios and measure their relative abundances.

The PVX-4110 is also useful for driving deflection plates in particle accelerators, letting researchers manipulate the trajectory of charged particles and guide them through the accelerator with greater accuracy.

Other applications for the PVX-4110 include driving power tube grids in high-power RF systems such as radar and communications equipment, pulsing Pockels cells and Q switches in laser systems, driving acoustic transducers for ultrasonic imaging, pulsing microchannel plates for particle detection, and gating photomultiplier tubes and image intensifiers for low-light imaging.

title: April 19, 2023 – Antenna Advancements: How BNC is Revolutionizing Wireless Communication

An antenna is a device designed to transmit or receive electromagnetic waves, consisting of a conductive material shaped to radiate or receive energy in a particular direction. Antennas are used in radio and television broadcasting, mobile communications, radar, and satellite communication.

How Antennas Work

Antennas work by converting electrical energy into electromagnetic waves, and vice versa. An electrical current applied to an antenna creates a changing electric field, which creates a changing magnetic field; these combine to form an electromagnetic wave that radiates out. When an electromagnetic wave passes over an antenna, it induces an electrical current that can power a receiver. The shape and size of an antenna determine its radiation pattern.

Advancements in Antenna Technology

  • Miniaturization: antennas have become smaller and more compact, easier to integrate into devices such as smartphones, wearables, and IoT devices
  • Multi-band operation: designed to operate on multiple frequency bands, supporting standards such as 2G, 3G, 4G, and 5G
  • Smart antennas: use signal processing algorithms to dynamically adjust the radiation pattern to optimize signal quality and reduce interference
  • Beamforming: uses multiple antennas to focus transmission or reception in a particular direction, improving range and efficiency

Scintillators are materials that emit light when they absorb radiation, and they are widely used in radiation detection and medical imaging.

GAGG(Ce) is a high-density scintillator material with strong properties for photon detection. Its high photon yield and energy resolution make it well suited for use in medical imaging, gamma spectroscopy, and Compton electron detection. The material is also non-hygroscopic, meaning it does not absorb moisture from the environment, making it a more reliable and stable choice where consistent performance is critical.

In medical imaging, GAGG(Ce) supports applications including positron emission tomography (PET), single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), and computed tomography (CT) imaging, where it can detect the gamma rays and Compton electrons emitted by radioactive tracers used to visualize internal organs and tissues.

In gamma spectroscopy, the high energy resolution and photon yield of GAGG(Ce) allow accurate measurement of the energy and intensity of gamma rays emitted by radioactive isotopes. Compton electron detection, important in fields including radiation therapy and environmental monitoring, is another application where GAGG(Ce)'s properties make it a useful tool.

title: April 5, 2023 – The Role of Cerium Bromide Scintillator CeBr3 in Real-Time Measurement While Drilling
body:
Measurement while drilling (MWD) is a technology used in the oil and gas industry to provide real-time information about the wellbore while drilling. MWD tools are located directly above the drill bit and measure parameters such as temperature, pressure, and drilling direction, transmitting the data gathered to the surface in real time so operators can make immediate decisions to optimize drilling performance and avoid problems.

One of the key components of MWD tools is the scintillation detector, used to measure the natural gamma radiation emitted by surrounding rock formations. Cerium Bromide (CeBr3) scintillator is a common choice for MWD applications because of its high light yield and fast response time.

Properties of Cerium Bromide Scintillator CeBr3

CeBr3 is a crystal in the halide family, with a high atomic number and high density, making it an effective detector of gamma radiation. The scintillator emits light when gamma rays interact with it, detected by photomultiplier tubes (PMTs). CeBr3 has a high light yield, producing a large number of photons per unit of energy deposited for better detection efficiency, and a fast response time that supports real-time measurement. It also has strong energy resolution, allowing for accurate identification of different isotopes and geological formations.

Role of Cerium Bromide Scintillator CeBr3 in MWD

MWD tools typically place a scintillation detector close to the drill bit to measure the gamma radiation emitted by surrounding rock formations, which comes from naturally occurring isotopes such as uranium, thorium, and potassium. By measuring it, MWD tools can determine the lithology and structure of the formations being drilled, helping operators make informed decisions about drilling performance and avoid problems such as getting stuck or drilling into a formation that could damage the drill bit.

title: March 21, 2023 – Scintillation Crystals for PET: What You Need to Know
body:
Scintillation crystals are materials that emit light when exposed to radiation. In PET imaging, they detect the gamma rays emitted by the radioactive tracers used in the procedure. When a gamma ray interacts with a scintillation crystal, it produces a burst of light that a photodetector detects and converts into an electrical signal, which is used to create the PET image.

Types of Scintillation Crystals Used in PET

Several types of scintillation crystals are commonly used in PET imaging. The most common are bismuth germanate (BGO) and lutetium oxyorthosilicate (LSO).

BGO crystals have been used in PET imaging for more than 30 years, known for high light output and strong energy resolution, and they are relatively inexpensive with a long lifespan.

LSO crystals are a more recent development, offering higher light output, better energy resolution, and faster decay time than BGO, which makes them well suited to high-resolution PET detectors.

Other scintillation crystals used in PET imaging include lutetium-yttrium oxyorthosilicate (LYSO), which is similar to LSO but has higher density and better energy resolution, and sodium iodide (NaI), which was used in PET imaging in the past but has largely been replaced by newer scintillation crystals due to lower light output and poorer energy resolution.

Advantages of Scintillation Crystals in PET Imaging

  • High sensitivity: scintillation crystals are highly sensitive to radiation, allowing them to detect even small amounts of radioactive material
  • High energy resolution: scintillation crystals can distinguish between different types of radiation based on energy level, supporting more accurate detection and measurement of radioactive tracers
  • Fast response time: scintillation crystals produce light almost immediately when exposed to radiation, supporting real-time imaging in PET scans
  • Low noise: scintillation crystals produce very little background noise, which improves the signal-to-noise ratio in PET imaging

title: March 20, 2023 – Model 875: Multi-Channel Radar Signal Generation with Precise Phase and Timing Accuracy
body:

Pulse Descriptor Word

Engineers conducting radar testing need to generate multi-pulse streams, with each pulse defined by parameters such as amplitude, frequency, phase, pulse width, time position, and intrapulse modulation or chirping. These parameters are collectively known as the pulse descriptor word (PDW), and a list of PDWs describes a radar pulse stream.

Multi-patch radar antenna arrays require additional parameters to be fully characterized, including inter-channel phase coherence, phase-coherent switching (where the relative phase between channels is stored in memory), and inter-channel timing accuracy.

Modes of Signal Generation

Berkeley Nucleonics' VSGs offer two modes for generating pulse descriptor words. In sequential PDW playback, a precompiled list of PDWs is uploaded into the internal memory of the Model 875 through Ethernet or USB; during playback, each PDW is translated into its corresponding modulation parameters sequentially and in real time. In PDW live-streaming, individual PDWs are sequentially fed into internal memory in real time through the Model 875 FCP for immediate playback.

Key Features and Performance

Generating radar pulse sequences that mimic real sequences depends on fast switching, phase coherence, and precise inter-channel timing, all important for implementing correct radar beam angle specifications in multi-channel systems. title: March 17, 2023 – Gamma Spectroscopy: The Role of Photomultiplier Tubes and Scintillator Detectors in Detecting Radioactive Emissions
body:
Gamma spectroscopy is an important technique used in many fields, including nuclear physics, medical imaging, and materials science. This technique relies on the detection and analysis of gamma rays emitted from radioactive sources, using specialized instruments such as photomultiplier tubes and scintillator detectors.

Photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) are one type of detector commonly used in gamma spectroscopy. These devices are highly sensitive light sensors that detect the faint flashes of light produced when gamma rays interact with matter. When a gamma ray interacts with a scintillator material, it produces a burst of light. A photomultiplier tube then detects this light, amplifies the signal, and converts it into an electrical signal that can be analyzed by a computer or other electronic device.

PMTs consist of a vacuum tube with a photocathode at one end and an anode at the other. When light enters the tube through a window, it strikes the photocathode and produces a stream of electrons, which are accelerated toward the anode by an electric field, causing them to collide with other atoms and produce even more electrons. This process repeats multiple times, resulting in a highly amplified electrical signal that can be measured and analyzed.

Scintillator detectors are another type of detector commonly used in gamma spectroscopy. These detectors use a scintillating material that produces light when it interacts with gamma rays, and a photodetector, such as a PMT or a photodiode, then converts that light into an electrical signal for analysis.

Several types of scintillator materials are used in gamma spectroscopy, including inorganic crystals such as sodium iodide and cesium iodide, as well as organic scintillators such as anthracene and stilbene, each with its own properties suited to specific applications. Scintillator detectors can be made in a variety of shapes and sizes, making them versatile for different types of experiments, and they are relatively easy to use with minimal maintenance compared to other detector types.

title: March 13, 2023 – Understanding the Basics of Phase Noise Testing: A Guide for Beginners
body:
Phase noise is the noise present in the phase of a signal relative to a reference signal. It is usually expressed in dBc/Hz, representing the noise power relative to the carrier power per unit of frequency. Phase noise can affect the performance of electronic systems, especially in applications where high accuracy and stability are required, such as wireless communication, radar, and frequency synthesis.

Why Phase Noise Testing Matters

Phase noise testing is essential to ensure the stability and accuracy of electronic systems, especially in high-frequency applications. Phase noise can reduce the signal-to-noise ratio, degrade the accuracy of frequency measurements, and increase the bit error rate in communication systems. Testing helps engineers identify and mitigate sources of phase noise, such as power supply noise, oscillator noise, and environmental factors.

How Phase Noise Testing Is Done

Phase noise testing can be performed using several techniques, including spectrum analyzers, phase noise analyzers, and oscilloscopes. Spectrum analyzers are the most common instruments used, since they provide a wide frequency range and high dynamic range measurements.

The basic procedure involves measuring the power spectrum of the signal under test (SUT) and of a reference signal, then comparing the two spectra at different offsets from the carrier frequency, typically ranging from a few Hz to several MHz. The phase noise spectrum is usually plotted as noise power density (dBc/Hz) versus frequency offset (Hz) from the carrier, revealing characteristics of the noise sources such as flicker noise, white noise, and spurious noise.

Choosing a Phase Noise Analyzer

Berkeley Nucleonics' 7300 Series phase noise analyzers offer a frequency range of up to 40 GHz, suitable for applications from basic research to complex communication systems, with high-resolution measurements and a low measurement floor for accurate detection of low-level phase noise, advanced temperature control and phase-locked loop technology for stability and repeatability, and an interface and analysis tools designed to help engineers interpret and optimize their results.

title: March 6, 2023 – Pulsed Power: Definition and Industry Applications
body:
Pulsed power is a technology that uses short but powerful electrical pulses to enable applications across numerous industries, from automotive manufacturing and food processing to military equipment and medical treatments.

As a supplier of high-voltage products, Berkeley Nucleonics provides pulsed power solutions to customers in medical, military, research, energy, and other industries. Our high-voltage pulse generators are built for applications that require longer pulse lengths and higher voltages.

The science of pulsed power involves technology, experimental tools, and capabilities that concentrate electrical energy in time and space so it can be harnessed for a range of applications. To create high-energy pulses, low-power electrical energy is stored in a bank of capacitors and released as short pulses at much higher power. As the pulse duration is shortened, in some cases to billionths of a second, the power increases, producing a very short but potent burst of energy.

Pulsed power finds use across a wide range of industries and technologies, including photomultiplier tubes and image intensifiers, UV light protection, electroporation, dielectric barrier discharge, atmospheric pressure plasma jets, time of flight, beam steering, Pockels cells, microchannel plates, Q-switches, acoustic transducers, industrial plasma generation, and X-ray generation for medical diagnostics and treatment.

High-voltage pulse generators play a central role in harnessing this energy and delivering the power needed for these applications, and Berkeley Nucleonics remains committed to providing pulsed power solutions to support them.

title: March 1, 2023 – Model 685 Series: AWGs for Optics, Photonics, and Lasers
body:
Applications based on optics, photonics, and lasers are becoming increasingly popular, opening new territory for real-world use, including lidar for automotive, medical solutions, aerospace and defense, quantum research, and laser sensors.

Testing challenges, time-to-market pressure, and increasingly demanding applications have made modern arbitrary waveform and function generators the right choice to meet these needs. AWGs give engineers a flexible, powerful instrument for producing all types of pulses, signals, and modulations. The Model 685 Series targets key issues in generating pulses for optics, photonics, and laser applications, accelerating testing, reliability, and characterization of optics and photonics systems.

Electro-optic Modulators

Integrated-optical waveguides guide light along a determined path, similar to optical fiber, with light guided by total internal reflection at the channel walls. The linear electro-optic effect, or Pockels effect, is a second-order non-linear effect in which the refractive index of an optical material changes when an external electric field is applied. Lithium niobate (LiNbO3) is the preferred material for fabricating integrated-optical modulators; applying an electric field to a waveguide via electrodes produces a phase shift in the guided light that is linear to the applied voltage. Because of the fast electro-optic response, low control voltages, and sophisticated electrode geometry, modulation at gigahertz frequencies is achievable.

The Model 685 Arbitrary Waveform Generator can create the modulation voltage by generating very narrow pulses, with a minimum pulse width of 230 ps, at amplitudes of up to 5 Vpp. Combined with a rise/fall time of 110 ps, this allows direct driving of many electro-optical modulators without an external amplifier. The True-Arb user interface makes it straightforward to generate a range of pulse shapes for finer control of the optical output signal.

Quantum Optics

Color centers in diamond are defects in the crystal lattice that act as promising solid-state quantum emitters for future quantum information processing and quantum networks. Recent research into group IV vacancy centers in diamond, particularly SiV and SnV centers, shows promising results for both single-photon generation and emitter spin coherence times, two of the typical challenges of working with solid-state quantum emitters.

The Model 685 has been used to control the experimental pulse sequences used to manipulate single tin-vacancy centers in diamond, generating narrow electrical square pulses to drive an electro-optical amplitude modulator and produce short laser pulses with a near-Gaussian shape. It has also been used to drive an electro-optical phase modulator to generate frequency sidebands, enabling two optical transitions to be driven with phase-stable laser fields. Its digital output channels can control acousto-optical amplitude modulators or generate trigger pulses for timing experimental sequences.

Pulsed Laser Diode Driver

The ability of pulsed laser diodes to deliver short, intense bursts of power has made them well suited to applications such as target designation and range-finding, with improved technology and lower costs now opening applications in metrology and medicine.

Pulsed laser diodes are driven with high-current pulses that produce short, high-power optical pulses, generally at a low duty cycle to reach very high peak optical powers. Producing these pulses requires currents on the order of several tens of amperes, requiring fast switching transistors and appropriate circuitry.

Many pulsed-laser-diode applications are variants of rangefinding, in which target distance is calculated from the flight time of a laser pulse reflected from the target, used in automotive collision-avoidance systems, navigational aids for ships, ceilometers for cloud-height measurement at airports, surveying and construction, laser safety scanners around hazardous industrial areas, intelligent highway systems, and medical laser therapy.

The Model 685 can directly control a pulsed laser diode, or control it indirectly through an electro-optic or acousto-optic modulator, creating rectangular, Gaussian, and exponential pulse shapes at amplitudes up to 5 Vpp with 110 ps rise and fall times and a minimum pulse width of 230 ps.

Conclusion

The Model 685 provides a flexible, high-performance solution for generating the pulses and signals needed to meet today's challenges in quantum optics, photonics, and laser applications.

title: February 8, 2023 – BNC Product Launch | 22GHz Compact Multi-Channel Phase-Coherent Frequency Synthesizer
body:
Berkeley Nucleonics (BNC) presents the Model 805, a compact frequency synthesizer that delivers precise, stable frequencies from 100 kHz to 22 GHz. One of its standout features is the ability to link multiple units for phase coherence and multi-channel operation. The Model 805 is user-friendly, and its compact design suits integration into a range of RF/microwave system layouts.

Single-Channel Performance

The Model 805 covers 100 kHz to 22 GHz with a resolution of 10 mHz using BNC's graphical control software, and finer resolution via SCPI commands. Switching time is 5 microseconds, and calibrated frequency accuracy is ±30 ppb with ±0.5 ppm aging in the first year, thanks to its OCXO reference. Output power is adjustable from -40 to +25 dBm with ±1.5 dB accuracy and 0.5 dB resolution, and phase can be adjusted from 0 to 360 degrees in 0.1-degree steps. Phase noise at a 20 kHz offset from a 1 GHz carrier is -132 dBc/Hz, and -110 dBc/Hz at a 100 Hz offset, with subharmonics and spurious signals below -55 dBc.

Beyond CW output, the Model 805 supports pulse modulation, either internally programmed or externally triggered, with a maximum modulation rate of 10 MHz and a narrowest pulse width of 30 ns. A high-speed triggered parameter-sweeping function with flexible sweep profiles is available, with a shortest step time of 5 microseconds. The synthesizer is housed in a well-shielded, flange-mountable module measuring 134 x 95 x 25 mm, weighs under 0.5 kg, and consumes only 17 W, allowing passive heat sinking with flexible mounting.

Multi-Channel and Phase-Coherent Operation

The Model 805 supports external references at 100 MHz and 1 GHz with a frequency lock range of ±10 ppm, and provides a 1 GHz reference output so multiple units can be linked for phase-coherent operation: the first unit acts as the reference, with its 1 GHz signal looped through the others. In testing, two daisy-chained Model 805 modules in a phase-coherent configuration at 5 GHz showed a relative phase difference variation of ±0.5 degree over 10 hours in a non-air-conditioned room. A low-noise amplifier between the 1 GHz reference input and output, with low additive phase noise, allows configurations of up to 16 phase-coherent channels.

Applications

The Model 805 serves as a clock for RF/microwave systems, particularly where multi-channel, phase-coherent local oscillators are required, and its per-channel phase adjustment supports precise timing alignment. Its phase-coherent, multi-channel configuration suits the design and testing of radar receivers, phased array beamforming networks, I/Q modulators in quantum computing instrumentation, MIMO receivers, and heterodyne spectroscopic systems, while its phase coherence and fast switching support fast frequency hopping in agile electronic warfare systems.

title: January 16, 2023 – The History of Gamma-ray Spectroscopy for Isotope Identification, J. McQuaid
body:
Gamma rays were first discovered and studied in 1900 by French chemist Paul Villard, while observing radiation from radium. The first quantitative analysis of gamma radiation is credited to Rutherford and Andrade in 1914, using diffraction spectroscopy with a rock-salt crystal.

Crystal diffraction was an important, pioneering effort in analyzing gamma-ray energy, but it fell short of providing a means to accurately quantify and identify various radionuclides. Several decades passed before scientists developed what we now know as gamma spectroscopy.

Gamma-ray Spectroscopy

A spectrometer system for radionuclide analysis is composed of a photon detector and associated electronics, such as an amplifier and pulse-shaping circuitry, along with a means of sorting various energy events and recording or displaying the data. These events are sorted to produce a spectrum, or histogram, displaying intensity of events as a function of photon energy.

The advent of the sodium-iodide scintillator in 1948, and other detectors that followed, made spectroscopy practical. The photon detector and the Multichannel Pulse-Height Analyzer (MCA) became the primary tools needed to produce a pulse-height spectrum of one or more radionuclides.

One of the first MCAs was developed by Fred Goulding in the 1950s at the Atomic Energy of Canada's Chalk River facility. This MCA, called a "Kicksorter," boasted excellent linearity and 100 channels. Goulding later worked at the Lawrence Berkeley Lab starting in 1959, bringing some of that early nuclear counting technology to the Berkeley and Livermore labs. In the years since, advances in MCAs have been substantial, with 16K-channel analyzers now common. Improvements in nuclear detectors have brought improved energy resolution, driving further advances in nuclear science; in the early 1960s, germanium detectors were developed with excellent energy resolution, and that work has continued with an emphasis on higher purity and larger ingots. Because these detectors require cooling to liquid nitrogen temperatures, advances in room-temperature detectors have been necessary to produce small, portable Radioisotope Identification Devices (RIIDs).

Berkeley Nucleonics Corporation (BNC) has been a leader in providing RIIDs for over two decades. One technique BNC has implemented is Quadratic Compression Conversion (QCC), a digital conversion transform used to obtain characterization of spectral peaks. QCC extends sensitivity beyond conventional spectroscopy by spreading out tightly spaced low-energy peaks and enhancing high-energy peaks, allowing for a faster and easier search of energy lines across the spectrum, which is especially important for quickly flagging highly enriched weapons-grade material. QCC is incorporated in BNC's SAM 940+ RIID, a lightweight, hand-held instrument that uses newer high-resolution detectors along with the capability for automatic software updates.

title: January 16, 2023 – New RF Power Sensors from Berkeley Nucleonics: High-Performance Measurement for Telecommunications, Broadcasting, and Research
body:
Berkeley Nucleonics Corporation (BNC), a provider of precision test and measurement instruments, developed several USB RF power sensors, expanding its RF/Microwave product line. These sensors are designed to measure RF power levels from 9 kHz to 50 GHz with a wide dynamic range, making them useful across a variety of applications, including telecommunications, broadcasting, industrial and scientific R&D, IoT and 5G/Wi-Fi, radar, and SatCom.

The Model 12xxx Series of sensors perform highly accurate power measurements of both CW and pulsed signals, with a range of features packed into the software GUI. The rugged enclosure makes them suitable for both laboratory and field environments, and the software offers plug-and-play simplicity along with a rich feature set.

"We are excited to offer customers these high-performance USB RF power sensors," said John Lauder, CTO of Berkeley Nucleonics Corporation. "These sensors will be a valuable tool for researchers, engineers, and technicians working in a wide range of fields."

BNC's RF power sensors can be ordered through the company's website or by contacting a regional sales representative. Technical support and an online training course on power measurements are also available.

title: December 27th, 2022 – What is an RF Power Sensor?
body:
An RF power sensor is a device that measures the power of a radio frequency (RF) signal. These sensors are used for a variety of applications, including determining the output power of a transmitter, monitoring RF signals for transmission or reception, and measuring the intensity of RF signals in a laboratory setting. RF power sensors are available across a wide range of frequency bands and can be used with various RF devices.

How Does an RF Power Sensor Work?

RF power sensors generally have a port, such as a coaxial connector, that allows them to be connected to the RF signal source. The sensor then measures the power of the RF signal and outputs a corresponding electrical signal, such as a voltage or current, which is then measured to determine the power of the RF signal.

Types of RF Power Sensors

  • Thermal sensors: use a small piece of thermally conductive material heated by the RF signal, with power calculated from the amount of heat generated
  • Diode sensors: use a diode to rectify the RF signal into a DC voltage proportional to the power of the RF signal
  • Calibrated sensors: calibrated to measure the power of an RF signal over a specific frequency range, typically combining the methods above with additional circuitry for accurate measurement

RF power sensors are used across a wide range of industrial applications, including testing and manufacturing of RF devices such as transmitters, antennas, and amplifiers; wireless communication signal strength measurement; radiofrequency identification (RFID); radar detection systems; medical equipment such as MRI machines; and industrial process control. These are just a few examples of the many industrial use cases for RF power sensors, which are also widely used in aerospace, defense, and telecommunications.

title: November 2nd, 2022 – How Far Away Can You Detect Radiation?
body:
If you hear a question like "how far away can you detect radiation," you know something is missing: what is the radioactive source, and what is its activity? How large is the detector, and what type of detector is being used? The sensitivity of the detector, the intensity of the radioactive source, and the type and energy of the radiation are all of central importance.

This article addresses scintillation detector efficiency versus sensitivity, along with other parameters affecting the detection of photon radiation, namely gamma-ray and X-ray spectra.

Detector Efficiency

Photon radiation, such as gamma rays, carries no charge, unlike alpha and beta particles. As a result, photon radiation must undergo a significant interaction within the detector before detection is possible, and because it may travel large distances before that interaction takes place, detector efficiency can be a small fraction of 100%. Describing the efficiency of a detector requires two classes of counting efficiency: absolute and intrinsic. Geometry and distance from the source to the detector greatly affect the accuracy of the calculated absolute efficiency, while intrinsic efficiency is calculated using the solid angle subtended from the source to the detector.

A more practical measurement used in spectroscopy is peak efficiency, which uses the full energy of the photopeak, counting only full-energy photopeak events. When other extraneous counts, such as small scattered events, are subtracted from the total photopeak, the resulting efficiency is called intrinsic peak efficiency, also referred to as net-peak efficiency, which is the most common efficiency measurement used for gamma-ray detectors and is important because it can be used to calculate the absolute activity of a radioactive source.

Detector Efficiency and Sensitivity

Detector efficiency and sensitivity are related when considering certain detector material properties, such as atomic number, light output, and matched wavelength. Sensitivity speaks more to a detector's degree of response to a stimulus, in this case the photon energy incident on the detector. A large detector exposed to a greater number of photons will generally exhibit a higher degree of sensitivity, assuming similar detector materials for comparison, though for some photon energies a smaller detector can have higher efficiency than a larger detector when comparing different detector materials, while the larger detector may still have greater detection sensitivity.

Sensitivity is often the most important factor in surveillance mode, since a radioactive source must be found before identification can take place. Sensitivity can be compromised with lanthanum-based materials because of intrinsic radiation from lanthanum-138 and actinium-227, which produces a high background across the spectrum, a loss of sensitivity that is particularly noticeable when sources are weak or at a distance. Shielded sources may also be difficult to recognize by their gamma structure due to high intrinsic background, photon absorption in the shielding, and electron scatter, even though efficiency is quite high.

Summary

It is important to use the proper term when describing a measurement or working toward a specific mission goal, accounting for factors such as geometry and possible sources of measurement error.
